pearl: Central white matter is composed of myelinated axons ("wires") traveling in parallel bundles to connect different gray matter processing regions.

stem: A neurohistology lecture compares the microscopic constituents of cerebral gray matter versus white matter. Which microscopic elements are concentrated in gray matter but virtually absent in central white matter tracts?

choices.B: Neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses

rationale: Gray matter contains concentrated neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses, whereas white matter consists predominantly of myelinated axons and supporting myelinating glia.
pearl: Gray matter contains concentrated neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses, whereas white matter consists predominantly of myelinated axons and supporting myelinating glia.

stem: A neuroanatomist examines a coronal brain section, identifying the boundary where the outer cerebral cortex transitions into underlying white matter. What microscopic structural change marks the junction between cerebral gray matter and white matter?

choices.A: Transition from regions containing cell bodies/synapses to regions consisting of dense myelinated axon bundles
choices.B: Transition from neural tube tissue to neural crest tissue
choices.C: Appearance of Schwann cells and peripheral ganglia
choices.D: Transition from solid tissue to cerebrospinal fluid
choices.E: Loss of blood vessels and appearance of meningeal membranes

rationale: The junction between gray and white matter marks the transition from regions containing neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses (gray matter) to regions consisting of dense myelinated axon bundles (white matter).
pearl: The junction between gray and white matter marks the transition from regions containing neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, and synapses (gray matter) to regions consisting of dense myelinated axon bundles (white matter).

stem: A neurotology researcher maps the distribution of chemical synapses within the central nervous system. Which anatomical regions of the cerebrum house these synaptic processing hubs?

choices.B: Outer cerebral cortex and deep gray nuclei (caudate, lentiform, thalamus, hypothalamus)

rationale:
Synaptic integration occurs within gray matter structures, which include both the outer cerebral cortex and deep gray nuclei (caudate, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, hypothalamus).

6. Section 6: Neuromuscular Junction (NMJ) Disorders & Cholinergic Pharmacology (Questions 151�180)

6.1 Acetylcholinesterase Biomarkers & Pathophysiology (Questions 151�158)
pearl: Synaptic integration occurs within gray matter structures, which include both the outer cerebral cortex and deep gray nuclei (caudate, lentiform nucleus, thalamus, hypothalamus).

stem: Mrs. Rogers undergoes prenatal screening during her 15th week of pregnancy. Laboratory evaluation of amniotic fluid obtained via amniocentesis demonstrates elevated levels of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP). Fetal MRI confirms a lumbosacral vertebral defect with a protruding sac containing malformed spinal cord tissue. What pathophysiological mechanism causes acetylcholinesterase to leak into the amniotic fluid?

choices.A: Increased maternal hepatic synthesis of AChE
choices.B: Direct leakage of central nervous tissue proteins/enzymes through an open neural tube defect into amniotic fluid
choices.C: Impaired fetal renal clearance of systemic proteins
choices.D: Premature degradation of fetal peripheral nerve myelin by Schwann cells

rationale: In open neural tube defects (such as open myelomeningocele or anencephaly), central nervous tissue is exposed directly to the external amniotic environment. This allows central neural enzymes and fetal proteins�specifically acetylcholinesterase (AChE) and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)�to leak directly into the amniotic fluid, elevating their concentrations.
pearl: In open neural tube defects (such as open myelomeningocele or anencephaly), central nervous tissue is exposed directly to the external amniotic environment.

stem: A 24-year-old pregnant woman at 16 weeks gestation undergoes amniocentesis after an initial maternal serum screening shows elevated alpha-fetoprotein. Diagnostic amniotic fluid testing confirms elevated acetylcholinesterase activity. Why is amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase considered a highly specific diagnostic marker for open neural tube defects compared to alpha-fetoprotein alone?

choices.A: Acetylcholinesterase is synthesized exclusively by placental trophoblasts
choices.B: Acetylcholinesterase is derived specifically from exposed neural tissue
choices.C: Alpha-fetoprotein is elevated only in lysosomal storage diseases
choices.D: Acetylcholinesterase is produced by the fetal liver in response to folic acid

rationale: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is an enzyme specific to nervous tissue synapses. Its presence in amniotic fluid specifically confirms an open neural tube defect, as exposed central neural tissue leaks AChE directly into the surrounding amniotic fluid.
pearl: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is an enzyme specific to nervous tissue synapses.

stem: A pregnant woman at 16 weeks gestation undergoes prenatal evaluation. Fetal imaging demonstrates a lumbosacral neural tube defect, and amniocentesis confirms elevated acetylcholinesterase. Which specific neural tube defect category causes elevated acetylcholinesterase in amniotic fluid?

choices.A: Closed, skin-covered meningocele with intact integument
choices.B: Open myelomeningocele with exposed neural tissue
choices.D: Chiari I malformation without spinal defect

rationale: Acetylcholinesterase leaks into amniotic fluid specifically when a neural tube defect is open (e.g., open myelomeningocele or anencephaly), allowing direct communication between exposed neural tissue and amniotic fluid. Closed, skin-covered defects do not leak central neural proteins into amniotic fluid.
pearl: Acetylcholinesterase leaks into amniotic fluid specifically when a neural tube defect is open (e.

stem: A maternal-fetal medicine specialist orders laboratory biomarkers for a second-trimester pregnant patient to evaluate for potential neural tube defects. Which two primary biomarkers measured in amniotic fluid confirm the diagnosis of an open neural tube defect?

choices.E: Folic acid and Sonic Hedgehog protein

rationale: The two classic diagnostic biomarkers for open neural tube defects are Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and Acetylcholinesterase (AChE).
pearl: The two classic diagnostic biomarkers for open neural tube defects are Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and Acetylcholinesterase (AChE).

stem: Amniocentesis performed at 16 weeks gestation in a high-risk pregnancy reveals completely normal levels of acetylcholinesterase and alpha-fetoprotein. Which developmental anomaly is ruled out by normal amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase levels?

choices.A: Open neural tube defect (e.g., open myelomeningocele)

rationale: Normal amniotic fluid levels of acetylcholinesterase rule out an open neural tube defect, as open NTDs characteristically release AChE into amniotic fluid.
pearl: Normal amniotic fluid levels of acetylcholinesterase rule out an open neural tube defect, as open NTDs characteristically release AChE into amniotic fluid.

stem: A researcher investigates the biochemical markers released by unclosed central nervous tissue in a fetal model of spina bifida. What synaptic enzyme enriched in central and peripheral nervous tissue is released into surrounding amniotic fluid when spinal cord tissue remains unclosed?
rationale: Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme concentrated in nervous tissue that leaks into amniotic fluid when neural tissue remains unclosed and exposed.
pearl: Acetylcholinesterase is an enzyme concentrated in nervous tissue that leaks into amniotic fluid when neural tissue remains unclosed and exposed.

stem: A pregnant woman receives prenatal counseling following elevated amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase results, indicating open neural tissue exposure. By what day of gestation should the neural tube normally close to prevent this neural tissue exposure?
rationale: The neural tube normally closes by day 27 of gestation. Failure of closure by this day leads to open NTDs and subsequent leakage of acetylcholinesterase.
pearl: The neural tube normally closes by day 27 of gestation.

stem: Diagnostic evaluation of amniotic fluid samples is conducted to distinguish open neural tube defects from abdominal wall defects or non-neural fetal anomalies. Elevated acetylcholinesterase in amniotic fluid distinguishes open myelomeningocele from which non-neural condition?

choices.A: Closed abdominal wall defects lacking exposed neural tissue
choices.E: All fetal conditions lacking exposed central nervous tissue

rationale:
Acetylcholinesterase is specific for neural tissue exposure; therefore, its elevation in amniotic fluid differentiates open NTDs from non-neural defects (or closed neural defects) where central nervous tissue is not exposed.

6.2 PNS Motor Pathways & Somatosensory Efferents (Questions 159�166)
pearl: Acetylcholinesterase is specific for neural tissue exposure; therefore, its elevation in amniotic fluid differentiates open NTDs from non-neural defects (or closed neural defects) where central nervous tissue is not exposed.

stem: A neurodevelopmental study maps motor output pathways extending from the spinal cord to peripheral skeletal muscles. Investigators trace motor neuron cell bodies in the spinal ventral horn and their axonal projections through peripheral nerves. Which embryonic structures give rise to spinal cord ventral horn motor neurons and peripheral nerve pathways, respectively?

choices.A: Ventral horn motor neurons from Neural Tube; peripheral nerve structures from Neural Crest
choices.B: Ventral horn motor neurons from Neural Crest; peripheral nerve structures from Neural Tube

rationale: Central nervous system motor neurons residing in the spinal cord ventral horn develop from the Neural Tube. Peripheral nervous system components, including sensory ganglia, autonomic fibers, and Schwann cells that coat peripheral nerves, develop from the Neural Crest.
pearl: Central nervous system motor neurons residing in the spinal cord ventral horn develop from the Neural Tube.

stem: A 10-year-old child suffers a traumatic laceration of the sciatic nerve in his right thigh, severing peripheral motor and sensory fibers. What myelinating cell type responsible for peripheral nerve repair and myelination is derived from the neural crest?
rationale: Schwann cells are peripheral myelinating glia derived from embryonic neural crest tissue.
pearl: Schwann cells are peripheral myelinating glia derived from embryonic neural crest tissue.

stem: An electromyography (EMG) study evaluates motor signal conduction from lower motor neuron cell bodies in the spinal cord out to the gastrocnemius muscle motor endplate. Where are the cell bodies of lower motor neurons located within the spinal cord gray matter?
rationale: Lower motor neuron cell bodies reside within the ventral horn of the spinal cord gray matter (derived from the neural tube).
pearl: Lower motor neuron cell bodies reside within the ventral horn of the spinal cord gray matter (derived from the neural tube).

stem: An embryologist traces somatosensory pathways, noting that primary sensory neuron cell bodies reside outside the spinal cord within dorsal root ganglia. Dorsal root sensory ganglia are derived from which embryonic structure?
rationale: Primary sensory neurons in dorsal root ganglia belong to the peripheral nervous system and originate from the neural crest.
pearl: Primary sensory neurons in dorsal root ganglia belong to the peripheral nervous system and originate from the neural crest.

stem: A newborn infant with a caudal spinal malformation presents with flaccid weakness of both lower extremities. Dysfunction of motor output in this infant reflects disruption of nerve pathways originating in which central spinal cord region?
rationale: Flaccid motor weakness results from damage to lower motor neuron pathways originating in the ventral horn motor neurons of the spinal cord.
pearl: Flaccid motor weakness results from damage to lower motor neuron pathways originating in the ventral horn motor neurons of the spinal cord.

stem: A patient presents with a traumatic injury to peripheral motor nerves supplying skeletal muscles in the arm. Peripheral nerves belong to which division of the nervous system, and derived from which embryonic source?

choices.A: Central Nervous System; derived from Neural Tube
choices.B: Peripheral Nervous System; derived from Neural Crest
choices.C: Central Nervous System; derived from Neural Crest
choices.D: Peripheral Nervous System; derived from Neural Tube

rationale: Peripheral nerves belong to the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) and are formed by neural crest derivatives (along with axons extending from ventral horn motor neurons).
pearl: Peripheral nerves belong to the Peripheral Nervous System (PNS) and are formed by neural crest derivatives (along with axons extending from ventral horn motor neurons).

stem: A medical student traces the pathway of somatic motor transmission from the central nervous system to skeletal muscle fibers. Which structure serves as the chemical communication site between peripheral motor nerve terminals and skeletal muscle fibers?
rationale: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is the chemical synapse where motor nerve axon terminals communicate with skeletal muscle fibers.
pearl: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is the chemical synapse where motor nerve axon terminals communicate with skeletal muscle fibers.

stem: A neurohistology lab contrasts central white matter tracts with peripheral motor nerve roots. Which myelinating cells insulate central corticospinal tracts and peripheral motor roots, respectively?

choices.E: Both are insulated exclusively by Schwann cells

rationale:
Oligodendrocytes insulate Central Nervous System tracts, whereas Schwann cells insulate Peripheral Nervous System nerve roots and nerves.

6.3 Clinical Neuromuscular & Spinal Cord Segmental Deficits (Questions 167�174)
pearl: Oligodendrocytes insulate Central Nervous System tracts, whereas Schwann cells insulate Peripheral Nervous System nerve roots and nerves.

stem: Cameron, a newborn infant examined in Case 1, presents with a large lumbosacral myelomeningocele sac containing protruding meninges, CSF, and disorganized spinal cord tissue. Based on the anatomical location of this lower spinal cord lesion, which deficit pattern is expected in Cameron?

choices.A: Exclusive upper extremity motor loss with intact lower body function
choices.B: Impaired sensory and motor function of the lower body, as well as bowel and bladder dysfunction
choices.C: Complete loss of visual acuity with preserved spinal reflexes
choices.D: Isolated personality changes with intact lower limb motor strength

rationale: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele involves severe malformation of the lower spinal cord and spinal nerves. Structural disruption at lower spinal cord levels characteristically affects sensory and motor function of the lower body, as well as bowel and bladder function.
pearl: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele involves severe malformation of the lower spinal cord and spinal nerves.

stem: A 6-month-old infant with spina bifida in the lumbosacral region undergoes a comprehensive neurological exam. The physician documents flaccid weakness of lower extremity muscles, bilateral absence of ankle tendon reflexes, and loss of response to pinprick over the legs and perineum. Damage to which structural components within the lumbosacral sac accounts for these motor and sensory deficits?

choices.B: Lumbosacral spinal cord segments and spinal nerves

rationale: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele directly damages the lumbosacral spinal cord segments and descending spinal nerves within the herniated sac, producing lower extremity sensory loss, motor weakness, and reflex abnormalities.
pearl: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele directly damages the lumbosacral spinal cord segments and descending spinal nerves within the herniated sac, producing lower extremity sensory loss, motor weakness, and reflex abnormalities.

stem: A pediatric neurosurgeon discusses the anatomical implications of neural tube defect level with surgical residents, contrasting cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral myelomeningocele levels. What general anatomical rule dictates the distribution of sensory and motor deficits in spinal cord lesions?

choices.A: Deficits occur in body regions innervated by spinal cord segments at and below the level of the anatomical defect
choices.B: Deficits occur exclusively above the anatomical level of the defect
choices.C: Lower spinal cord defects selectively impair upper extremity function
choices.D: Deficits occur only in cranial nerve distributions
choices.E: Deficits are universally confined to visual perception

rationale: Neurological deficits resulting from spinal cord malformations or lesions occur in body regions at and below the level of the defect, due to disruption of segmental lower motor neurons/sensory inputs and descending/ascending spinal tracts.
pearl: Neurological deficits resulting from spinal cord malformations or lesions occur in body regions at and below the level of the defect, due to disruption of segmental lower motor neurons/sensory inputs and descending/ascending spinal tracts.

stem: An infant with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele is evaluated for neurogenic bladder and neurogenic bowel dysfunction. Why are bowel and bladder functions characteristically impaired in lower spinal cord (lumbosacral) malformations?

choices.A: Autonomous control of bowel and bladder resides in the prefrontal cortex
choices.B: Sacral spinal cord segments innervating bowel and bladder sphincters/autonomics are disrupted within the lumbosacral defect
choices.C: Bowel and bladder function depend on Schwann cells in the optic nerve
choices.D: Acetylcholinesterase is absent from smooth muscle
choices.E: Folic acid deficiency selectively paralyzes smooth muscle cells

rationale: Autonomic and somatic innervation controlling bowel and bladder function is mediated by sacral segments of the lower spinal cord. Lumbosacral myelomeningocele directly disrupts these sacral spinal cord segments and spinal nerves, leading to neurogenic bowel and bladder dysfunction.
pearl: Autonomic and somatic innervation controlling bowel and bladder function is mediated by sacral segments of the lower spinal cord.

stem: Examination of a newborn with an open lumbosacral myelomeningocele confirms lower extremity weakness and loss of tendon reflexes. What type of motor neuron lesion pattern is produced at the level of the myelomeningocele spinal cord defect?

choices.B: Lower motor neuron lesion (flaccidity, hypotonia, areflexia)

rationale: Direct structural destruction of ventral horn motor neurons and spinal nerves at the level of a myelomeningocele causes a lower motor neuron lesion pattern, characterized by muscle flaccidity, weakness, and loss of deep tendon reflexes (areflexia).
pearl: Direct structural destruction of ventral horn motor neurons and spinal nerves at the level of a myelomeningocele causes a lower motor neuron lesion pattern, characterized by muscle flaccidity, weakness, and loss of deep tendon reflexes (areflexia).

stem: A newborn infant with spina bifida develops overflow urinary incontinence, lack of lower limb movement, and sensory loss over the legs. What clinical triad defines lower spinal cord (lumbosacral) myelomeningocele?

choices.A: Lower limb sensory loss, lower limb motor weakness, and bowel/bladder dysfunction
choices.B: Hyperacusis, macrocephaly, and cherry-red macular spot
choices.C: "Wrinkled tissue paper" cells, bone pain, and splenomegaly
choices.D: Cough headaches, cervical syrinx, and cape-like sensory loss
choices.E: Cyclopia, proboscis, and single lateral ventricle

rationale: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele is defined by the clinical triad of lower limb sensory loss, lower limb motor weakness, and bowel/bladder dysfunction.
pearl: Lumbosacral myelomeningocele is defined by the clinical triad of lower limb sensory loss, lower limb motor weakness, and bowel/bladder dysfunction.

stem: A pediatric neurologist performs sensory pinprick testing on an infant with a lumbosacral neural tube defect, noting loss of nociceptive response below the L2 dermatome. What ascending spinal tract carrying pain and temperature is disrupted at and below the lumbosacral defect?
rationale: Sensory pathways carrying pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic tract, which is disrupted at and below the level of a myelomeningocele defect.
pearl: Sensory pathways carrying pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic tract, which is disrupted at and below the level of a myelomeningocele defect.

stem: Physical therapy evaluation of a 1-year-old child following neonatal repair of a lumbosacral myelomeningocele reveals preserved upper extremity and neck strength with paraparesis of both lower limbs. Preserved neck and arm motor strength in this child indicates normal function of which spinal cord segments?
rationale:
Normal upper limb (arm) and neck motor strength indicates that cervical spinal cord segments situated rostral (superior) to the lumbosacral defect are structurally normal and fully functional.

6.4 Cholinergic & Autonomic Signaling in Peripheral Ganglia (Questions 175�180)
pearl: Normal upper limb (arm) and neck motor strength indicates that cervical spinal cord segments situated rostral (superior) to the lumbosacral defect are structurally normal and fully functional.

stem: A pharmacological experiment evaluates neurotransmitter release across peripheral autonomic ganglia and the somatic neuromuscular junction. Which neurotransmitter is released by somatic lower motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction as well as preganglionic autonomic neurons?
rationale: Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter released by somatic motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction, as well as by preganglionic fibers within peripheral autonomic ganglia.
pearl: Acetylcholine is the primary neurotransmitter released by somatic motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction, as well as by preganglionic fibers within peripheral autonomic ganglia.

stem: An enzyme assay measures neurotransmitter breakdown within synaptic clefts at peripheral neuromuscular junctions and autonomic ganglia. What enzyme is responsible for rapidly hydrolyzing acetylcholine to terminate synaptic transmission at peripheral endplates?
rationale: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is the synaptic enzyme located in the synaptic cleft that rapidly hydrolyzes and inactivates acetylcholine, terminating synaptic signaling at neuromuscular endplates and cholinergic ganglia.
pearl: Acetylcholinesterase (AChE) is the synaptic enzyme located in the synaptic cleft that rapidly hydrolyzes and inactivates acetylcholine, terminating synaptic signaling at neuromuscular endplates and cholinergic ganglia.

stem: Histological sectioning of peripheral autonomic ganglia demonstrates postganglionic neuronal networks derived from neural crest cells. Neural crest cells give rise to which division of the peripheral nervous system mediating autonomic signaling?
rationale: Peripheral autonomic ganglia and fibers are derived from embryonic neural crest tissue.
pearl: Peripheral autonomic ganglia and fibers are derived from embryonic neural crest tissue.

stem: A neurophysiology research project compares action potential conduction velocity along myelinated somatic motor axons versus unmyelinated autonomic postganglionic fibers. What glial cell type synthesizes myelin sheaths for peripheral motor axons to enable rapid saltatory conduction?
rationale: Schwann cells synthesize myelin around peripheral motor axons, enabling rapid saltatory conduction along peripheral nerves.
pearl: Schwann cells synthesize myelin around peripheral motor axons, enabling rapid saltatory conduction along peripheral nerves.

stem: A toxicology study evaluates the synaptic effects of organophosphate exposure, which causes irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase at peripheral cholinergic synapses. What immediate biochemical event occurs at the neuromuscular junction when acetylcholinesterase is inhibited?

choices.A: Accumulation of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft causing continuous receptor stimulation
choices.B: Rapid depletion of acetylcholine from presynaptic vesicles
choices.C: Accumulation of glucocerebroside in motor endplates
choices.D: Selective destruction of peripheral Schwann cells
choices.E: Immediate re-closure of the central neural tube

rationale: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase prevents the breakdown of acetylcholine, leading to an accumulation of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, resulting in persistent, continuous stimulation of postsynaptic receptors.
pearl: Inhibiting acetylcholinesterase prevents the breakdown of acetylcholine, leading to an accumulation of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, resulting in persistent, continuous stimulation of postsynaptic receptors.

stem: A comprehensive review of peripheral nervous system embryology, histology, and neurochemistry summarizes peripheral neuromuscular system features. Which set correctly pairs embryonic tissue origin, peripheral glial cell type, primary motor neurotransmitter, and terminating enzyme for the peripheral neuromuscular system?

choices.A: Neural Crest origin -> Schwann cell glia -> Acetylcholine neurotransmitter -> Acetylcholinesterase degradation
choices.B: Neural Tube origin -> Oligodendrocyte glia -> Dopamine neurotransmitter -> Sphingomyelinase degradation
choices.C: Endoderm origin -> Astrocyte glia -> Serotonin neurotransmitter -> Hexosaminidase degradation
choices.D: Mesoderm origin -> Microglia glia -> Psychosine neurotransmitter -> Arylsulfatase degradation
choices.E: Notochord origin -> Ependymal glia -> Sulfatide neurotransmitter -> Beta-glucosidase degradation

rationale: Peripheral nervous system structures originate from the Neural Crest, are myelinated by Schwann cells, utilize Acetylcholine as the somatic motor neurotransmitter, and rely on Acetylcholinesterase for neurotransmitter breakdown and termination of synaptic signaling.
pearl: Peripheral nervous system structures originate from the Neural Crest, are myelinated by Schwann cells, utilize Acetylcholine as the somatic motor neurotransmitter, and rely on Acetylcholinesterase for neurotransmitter breakdown and termination of synaptic signaling.

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department at 3 AM after being ejected from a car. He is comatose, his right pupil is fixed and dilated, and his blood alcohol level is 0.33. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial imaging study?

choices.A: MRI of the brain with gadolinium

rationale: CT is fast, widely available, and the study of choice for acute trauma and suspected acute hemorrhage (epidural/subdural/SAH). A blown pupil suggests uncal herniation from an expanding mass lesion—time matters. MRI (A) takes longer and is less sensitive for hyperacute blood; skull films (B) are rarely indicated and miss intracranial pathology; angiography (D) and PET (E) are not trauma screening tools. Non-contrast is used because contrast can mimic/obscure blood.
pearl: "Comatose + fixed pupil → get a CT stat." CT = trauma, hemorrhage, initial stroke, skull fracture.

stem: A radiology resident reviews a non-contrast head CT. Which of the following correctly orders tissues from LEAST dense (darkest) to MOST dense (brightest)?

choices.A: Air → CSF → brain parenchyma → acute blood → bone
choices.B: CSF → air → acute blood → brain parenchyma → bone
choices.C: Air → brain parenchyma → CSF → bone → acute blood
choices.D: Air → CSF → acute blood → brain parenchyma → bone
choices.E: CSF → brain parenchyma → air → acute blood → bone

rationale: On CT, density (attenuation) increases from air (black) → fluid/CSF → soft tissue (brain) → blood (acute clot is hyperdense from concentrated hemoglobin/protein) → calcium/bone → metal (brightest).
pearl: "Air, fluid, soft tissue, blood, bone, metal" — darkest to brightest.

stem: A 19-year-old man is struck in the temple with a baseball bat. He loses consciousness briefly, wakes up and talks normally, then becomes progressively obtunded 2 hours later. CT would most likely show which of the following?

choices.B: Hyperdensity filling the basal cisterns and sylvian fissures
choices.C: Diffuse loss of gray-white differentiation with no extra-axial collection
choices.D: Hypodense crescent along the convexity with midline shift
choices.E: Biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdensity that does not cross suture lines

rationale: Temporal bone fracture with middle meningeal artery tear produces an epidural hematoma—a lens/lemon-shaped (biconvex) hyperdense collection limited by suture lines (dura is tightly adherent at sutures). Classic "lucid interval." Crescentic (A) = subdural; cisternal blood (B) = SAH; hypodense crescent (D) = chronic subdural.
pearl: Epidural = lens/lemon; Subdural = banana/crescent/sickle.

stem: A 75-year-old man has had several weeks of gradually worsening confusion, headaches, listlessness, and an unsteady gait. He denies trauma but takes apixaban. Non-contrast CT shows a left fronto-parietal extra-axial crescentic collection that is darker than adjacent brain, with 2–3 cm of midline shift. What is the approximate age of this collection?
rationale: Blood evolves on CT: hyperdense (acute, after ~30 min) → isodense (subacute, ~1–2 weeks) → hypodense (chronic, >2 weeks) as macrophages digest hemoglobin from the outside in. A hypodense crescent in an elderly patient with insidious symptoms = chronic subdural hematoma (bridging vein tear; atrophy and anticoagulation are risk factors).
pearl: Hyper → iso → hypo: acute → subacute (1–2 wk) → chronic (>2 wk). Thicker clots take longer to change.

stem: A neurosurgeon notes that the sensitivity of non-contrast CT for intracranial blood declines over time. Approximately what is the sensitivity of CT for detecting blood 2 weeks after a bleed?
rationale: Per lecture: poor in the immediate first 30 min, 85–95% at 1–24 h, ~80% at 3 days, ~50% at 1 week, and ~30% at 2 weeks. As hemoglobin breaks down, blood becomes iso- then hypodense and harder to distinguish—especially for SAH (where LP for xanthochromia may be needed).
pearl: The longer you wait, the less sensitive CT is for blood.

stem: A 68-year-old woman develops sudden right hemiparesis and aphasia 40 minutes ago. Head CT is unremarkable. Which MRI sequence would be most sensitive for confirming acute ischemic infarction at this time?
rationale: DWI detects restricted diffusion from cytotoxic edema within ~30 minutes of stroke onset; acute infarcts appear bright. T2/FLAIR may take several hours (~2+ h) to become abnormal. CT in the first 2–4 h shows only subtle changes, with maximal edema/shift at 3–5 days.
pearl: DWI bright + ADC dark = acute stroke. DWI positivity persists ~2 weeks → helps date stroke (acute vs chronic).

stem: An MRI of the brain is displayed in which the white matter is bright, the cortical gray matter is gray, and the CSF in the ventricles is dark. This sequence is best described as which of the following?
rationale: T1 images best depict normal neuroanatomy: white matter is white (fat-rich myelin), gray matter gray, CSF black ("T1 looks like the brain"). T2 reverses this (CSF bright, white matter dark). FLAIR is T2-like but with dark CSF.
pearl: "World War 2" — Water is White on T2.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has had an episode of painful monocular vision loss and, 1 year later, an episode of leg numbness. Her physician wants the most sensitive sequence to detect periventricular demyelinating plaques without CSF signal obscuring them. Which sequence is best?
rationale: FLAIR is a T2-based sequence in which CSF signal is suppressed (dark), so bright periventricular and subcortical white matter lesions are no longer obscured by adjacent bright CSF—the main pitfall of standard T2 (B). This makes FLAIR the workhorse for multiple sclerosis.
pearl: FLAIR = T2 with the CSF "turned off" → best for MS plaques.

stem: A patient with a suspected acute infarct has a lesion that is bright on DWI. The radiologist reviews an additional "add-on" map to confirm the lesion is truly acute rather than "T2 shine-through." On this map, an acute stroke would appear:
rationale: The apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) map quantifies water diffusion. In true acute ischemia, diffusion is restricted → low ADC → dark. A lesion bright on both DWI and ADC is T2 shine-through rather than true restriction.
pearl: Acute stroke: DWI bright / ADC dark.

stem: A non-contrast CT shows an ill-defined hypodense area in the left hemisphere. After IV contrast, a focal enhancing mass becomes obvious. Which of the following best explains why contrast improves lesion detection?

choices.A: Contrast is actively taken up by metabolically active neurons
choices.B: Contrast binds to myelin, making white matter more conspicuous
choices.C: Contrast increases CSF density, outlining the ventricles
choices.D: Contrast leaks across a disrupted blood-brain barrier into the lesion
choices.E: Contrast causes vasoconstriction of normal vessels, highlighting abnormal ones

rationale: Neither iodinated (CT) nor gadolinium (MRI) contrast crosses an intact BBB. Destructive processes—tumor (e.g., malignant glioma), abscess, acute stroke—disrupt tight junctions, letting contrast leak into the parenchyma ("enhancement"). Metabolic uptake (A) describes PET tracers.
pearl: Enhancement = BBB breakdown (tumor, abscess, infarct, active MS plaque).

stem: A 62-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease (eGFR 22) needs evaluation for a suspected intracranial aneurysm. Which study allows evaluation of the cerebral vessels without any IV contrast?
rationale: MRA can be performed without contrast (flow-based technique), making it useful in renal insufficiency or contrast allergy; gadolinium may be added to increase sensitivity. CTA (A) and catheter angiography (C) require iodinated contrast, which is more nephrotoxic than gadolinium.
pearl: MRA: no radiation, contrast optional. CTA: better spatial resolution but radiation + iodinated contrast.

stem: A 68-year-old woman is scheduled for a brain MRI to evaluate vertigo. Which of the following findings in her history is most important to address before the scan?
rationale: The strong magnetic field is the main MRI hazard. Most pacemakers are MRI-unsafe (some newer devices are MRI-conditional); many aneurysm clips and other metal implants/fragments must be screened. Cardiology should be involved for any implanted cardiac device. Iodinated contrast allergy (A) is irrelevant to gadolinium; claustrophobia (B) can be managed with benzodiazepines or an open MRI.
pearl: Screen for metal before MRI—pacemakers, aneurysm clips, orbital metal (skull X-ray can screen orbits).

stem: A 30-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation develops a new severe headache with focal neurologic deficits. Which imaging approach best balances diagnostic sensitivity with fetal safety?

choices.E: MRI with gadolinium as the first-line study

rationale: MRI uses no ionizing radiation and has no known adverse fetal effects, making it preferred in pregnancy. Gadolinium should be avoided in pregnancy if possible (E). CT, PET, and myelography expose the fetus to ionizing radiation.
pearl: Pregnant + needs imaging → MRI without gadolinium when possible.

stem: A 74-year-old man has new-onset vertigo, nystagmus, and gait ataxia. A non-contrast head CT in the ED is unremarkable. Why is an MRI still indicated?

choices.A: CT cannot detect hemorrhage after 1 hour
choices.B: MRI is faster and more widely available than CT
choices.C: CT poorly images the posterior fossa (brainstem and cerebellum)
choices.D: MRI is superior for detecting skull fractures
choices.E: CT exposes the patient to gadolinium

rationale: Dense petrous and occipital bone creates beam-hardening artifact in the posterior fossa, making CT insensitive for brainstem/cerebellar infarcts. MRI is far better for the posterior fossa. CT is better for bone (D), and is faster (B).
pearl: Posterior circulation stroke symptoms + normal CT → still get MRI (DWI).

stem: A 22-year-old man presents with fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity. He also has papilledema and a new left hemiparesis. Before lumbar puncture, which of the following CT findings would make LP contraindicated?

choices.C: Normal ventricles with a symmetric appearance
choices.D: A posterior fossa mass with obstructive hydrocephalus
choices.E: Mucosal thickening of the maxillary sinus

rationale: CT should precede LP whenever herniation is a risk (papilledema, focal deficits, altered mental status). Draining CSF from the lumbar cistern creates a pressure gradient that can precipitate tonsillar/transtentorial herniation. Mnemonic STOP: Shift (midline), Trauma, Obstruction (obstructive hydrocephalus—ventricles enlarged proximal to lesion), Posterior fossa mass.
pearl: Don't LP if CT shows Shift, Trauma, Obstruction, Posterior mass. Don't delay antibiotics for imaging in meningitis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer develops headaches, confusion, and memory loss. Head CT is equivocal. Which study is most appropriate to evaluate for metastatic disease?

choices.E: MRI of the brain with gadolinium

rationale: Contrast-enhanced MRI is superior to CT for metastases (smaller lesions, posterior fossa, enhancement with BBB disruption). Metastases tend to lodge at the gray-white junction, where arteries taper into arterioles and tumor emboli become trapped.
pearl: Brain mets: Breast, Bronchus (lung), Bowel, Kidney (+ melanoma). Gray-white junction.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has headaches, tinnitus, and right-sided sensorineural hearing loss. A contrast-enhanced T1 MRI shows a well-circumscribed, enhancing 2 × 2 cm mass at the cerebellopontine angle with a "tail" extending into the internal auditory canal. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.E: Epidermoid cyst of the fourth ventricle

rationale: A CPA mass extending into the internal auditory canal with unilateral SNHL and tinnitus is classic for vestibular schwannoma (CN VIII Schwann cells). Meningioma is the main differential (dural tail). Lecture point: CT showed only "soft signs"—this is why posterior fossa masses need contrast MRI.
pearl: CPA mass + unilateral hearing loss = schwannoma (bilateral → NF2).

stem: A 77-year-old woman has difficulty walking, progressive memory loss, and urinary incontinence. A non-contrast T1 MRI shows enlarged ventricles and generous cisterns with periventricular white matter changes, no mass effect, and no midline shift. Which imaging characteristic best supports normal pressure hydrocephalus over atrophy (hydrocephalus ex vacuo)?

choices.A: Ventricular enlargement out of proportion to sulcal enlargement
choices.C: Enlarged fourth ventricle with a posterior fossa mass
choices.D: Enlargement of only the lateral ventricles proximal to an obstruction at the foramen of Monro

rationale: In NPH (communicating hydrocephalus with "wet, wobbly, wacky"), ventricles are disproportionately enlarged relative to sulci. In diffuse cortical atrophy/ex vacuo, ventricles and sulci enlarge proportionally (B). D describes obstructive hydrocephalus. The lecture case was read as diffuse cortical atrophy with non-specific white matter disease—highlighting the need to compare ventricular vs sulcal size.
pearl: NPH: ventriculomegaly > sulcal enlargement; responds to LP/shunt.

stem: An 18-year-old pedestrian struck by a car is intubated and comatose. Non-contrast CT shows a 2 × 4 cm hyperdense extra-axial mass over the right parietal convexity, effacement of the right lateral ventricle, no visible sulcal pattern, and loss of the gray-white junction. Loss of the gray-white junction in this setting most strongly suggests which of the following?

choices.D: Diffuse cerebral edema/diffuse axonal injury with elevated ICP

rationale: Loss of gray-white differentiation and effacement of sulci/ventricles indicate diffuse cerebral swelling—seen with diffuse axonal injury (shearing) and severe TBI—implying elevated ICP and herniation risk. Lecture differential: epidural hematoma + TBI; "a life-threatening injury."
pearl: Systematic CT read: symmetry, gray-white differentiation, shift (mm), hyper/hypodensity, pneumocephalus, mass/foreign body.

stem: A neurosurgeon is planning a temporal lobectomy for refractory epilepsy and wants to map the patient's language and motor cortex preoperatively by detecting regional changes in cerebral blood flow during tasks. Which technique is most appropriate?
rationale: fMRI detects changes in blood flow/oxygenation (BOLD signal) to map active "eloquent" cortex (motor, language, vision) in presurgical candidates (tumor resection, temporal lobectomy). Lecture notes it is used primarily in research/neuropsychology clinically.
pearl: fMRI = blood flow mapping of activity; MEG = direct neuromagnetic signals with superior timing.

stem: A 58-year-old man treated with radiation for glioblastoma now has a new enhancing lesion at the resection site on MRI. The team needs to distinguish radiation necrosis from recurrent tumor. Which study is most helpful?
rationale: PET measures metabolic activity using a radiolabeled tracer (usually fluorine-18 FDG). Active tumor is hypermetabolic (high glucose uptake), whereas necrosis is hypometabolic. Lecture: PET "helps distinguish necrosis from active disease."
pearl: "My 18 PETs ate SPECks of iodized salt" — PET uses F-18; SPECT uses Tc-99m or iodine isotopes.

stem: Compared with PET, single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) is best characterized by which of the following?

choices.A: Uses fluorine-18 and has better spatial resolution
choices.C: Measures neuromagnetic fields directly from neurons
choices.D: Lower cost with lower contrast and spatial resolution; uses technetium-99m or iodine isotopes
choices.E: Is the study of choice for acute traumatic hemorrhage

rationale: PET has better contrast and spatial resolution; SPECT is cheaper with lower resolution and uses γ-emitters (Tc-99m, I-123, I-131). SPECT is used to localize seizure foci, evaluate brain injury, and localize tumors (antibody-linked tracers). C describes MEG.
pearl: SPECT: cheaper, seizure focus localization.

stem: Which imaging modality maps the electrical activity of neuronal populations by detecting the magnetic fields they generate, providing both spatial and precise timing information, and is available at only a handful of US centers?
rationale: MEG uses extraordinarily sensitive detectors to record neuromagnetic signals, giving direct spatial and temporal data—more powerful than fMRI for relating function to structure. Co-registration with MRI (MEG-MRI) requires specialized equipment and expertise.
pearl: fMRI = indirect (blood flow); MEG = direct (neuronal currents) with millisecond timing.

stem: A 55-year-old man with prior L4–S1 fusion with pedicle screws develops new radicular pain down the right leg. Metal artifact limits MRI. Which study is best to evaluate nerve root impingement?
rationale: Spinal MRI is generally the most sensitive study for cord and roots, but in patients with spinal hardware, CT myelogram is the alternative. Radiopaque contrast is injected intrathecally; roots appear as dark filling defects against bright contrast, revealing impingement. Contraindications: iodine allergy, significant renal dysfunction; relative: pregnancy. Can cause spinal headache.
pearl: Spinal hardware or MRI contraindicated → CT myelogram for nerve roots.

stem: A 60-year-old woman has hyperreflexia in both legs, a Babinski sign bilaterally, and loss of sensation below the umbilicus. She has no implanted devices. Which is the best imaging study?
rationale: Bilateral UMN signs with a sensory level at T10 (umbilicus) suggests thoracic cord compression—an indication for urgent imaging. Spinal MRI is the most sensitive modality for the cord, roots, discs, ligaments, tumors, and inflammation.
pearl: Suspected cord compression = urgent MRI spine. T10 dermatome = umbilicus.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus develops multifocal neurologic deficits. CNS vasculitis of small vessels is suspected, but MRA and CTA are unrevealing. Which study is most appropriate next?
rationale: Conventional (catheter-guided) angiography has the highest spatial resolution and can detect medium- to small-vessel vasculitis often too small for MRA or CTA. It is also used for aneurysm, AVM, and atherosclerosis evaluation, and can be combined with biopsy.
pearl: Small vessels missed on MRA/CTA → catheter angiography (gold standard).

stem: In an axial head CT, a lesion appears on the left side of the image. Which side of the patient's brain contains the lesion, and why?

choices.A: Left, because images are viewed from above the head
choices.B: Left, because CT is displayed in true anatomic orientation
choices.C: It cannot be determined without a sagittal image
choices.D: Right, because images are viewed from the patient's back
choices.E: Right, because images are viewed from the feet looking toward the head

rationale: By radiologic convention, axial images are viewed as if standing at the supine patient's feet looking up toward the head. Therefore the image's left side = patient's right side (and vice versa). Orientation errors are among the most common—and preventable—mistakes in image interpretation.
pearl: Radiologic convention: image left = patient right.

stem: A medical student reviewing a series of axial MRI slices from superior to inferior notes that the lateral sulcus is first oriented perpendicular to the lateral edge of the section, bordered by the parietal lobe. As slices descend, the lateral sulcus becomes more vertically oriented and a new lobe appears posteriorly. Which lobe appears?
rationale: Per Dr. Cohan's tutorial, the lateral sulcus slopes upward posteriorly into the parietal lobe. On higher axial cuts, the sulcus is adjacent to parietal lobe and perpendicular to the edge; as the plane descends, the temporal lobe gradually appears posteriorly—marked by a change to a more vertical sulcal orientation.
pearl: Axial: lateral sulcus perpendicular → parietal level; vertical → temporal lobe appears.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents 90 minutes after onset of left arm and face weakness. He is a candidate for thrombolysis. What is the primary purpose of obtaining an emergent non-contrast head CT?

choices.A: To identify the ischemic core with high sensitivity
choices.B: To exclude intracranial hemorrhage before thrombolysis

rationale: CT is fast and highly sensitive for acute hemorrhage. In acute stroke, a negative CT for blood allows consideration of thrombolysis. Ischemic changes are subtle at 2–4 h; maximal edema/shift appears at 3–5 days. CT perfusion/angiography can then show penumbra (increased time-to-peak) and large vessel occlusion (e.g., M1).
pearl: Stroke CT question = "rule out bleed before tPA."

stem: A contrast CT shows a 2.5 cm ring-enhancing intraparenchymal mass in the right parietotemporal lobe with marked edema and 1.5 cm midline shift. MRI shows the lesion's inner wall is thin and smooth with restricted diffusion centrally. Which diagnosis is favored?
rationale: Ring-enhancing lesion differential: metastasis, glioma (glioblastoma), abscess, lymphoma. Abscesses typically have a thin, smooth, uniform enhancing wall and central restricted diffusion (pus). Glioblastoma usually has a thick, irregular/ragged nodular rim with central necrosis. Pertinent questions to rule in abscess: fever, immunosuppression, dental/sinus/ear infection, endocarditis, IV drug use.
pearl: Ring-enhancing: smooth thin wall + DWI-bright center → abscess; irregular thick wall → GBM/met. Ragged hypodensity favors malignancy.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 34-year-old woman lightly touches her right index finger with a cotton swab. Where is the cell body of the first-order neuron carrying this information to the CNS?

choices.A: Posterior horn of the spinal cord
choices.D: Ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
choices.E: Anterior horn of the spinal cord

rationale: First-order sensory neurons are pseudounipolar with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion (a peripheral ganglion in the intervertebral foramen). The peripheral process innervates the receptor; the central process enters the cord via the dorsal root and ascends ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns. Nucleus cuneatus (C) = 2nd order; VPL (D) = 3rd order.
pearl: DCML: 1° DRG → 2° nucleus gracilis/cuneatus (caudal medulla) → 3° VPL thalamus → postcentral gyrus.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: In the dorsal column–medial lemniscus pathway, the second-order axons cross the midline at which location and via which fibers?

choices.A: Anterior white commissure of the spinal cord at the level of entry
choices.B: Rostral pons via the trapezoid body
choices.C: Midbrain via the decussation of the superior cerebellar peduncle
choices.D: Caudal medulla via the internal arcuate fibers

rationale: First-order axons synapse ipsilaterally on nucleus gracilis/cuneatus in the caudal medulla. Second-order axons sweep ventromedially as internal arcuate fibers, cross the midline (sensory decussation), and ascend contralaterally as the medial lemniscus. A describes spinothalamic (ALS) crossing.
pearl: DCML is ipsilateral in the cord and contralateral from the caudal medulla upward.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 45-year-old man has a small demyelinating lesion confined to the medial-most portion of the left dorsal column at the T4 cord level. Which deficit is expected?

choices.A: Loss of vibration and proprioception in the left leg
choices.B: Loss of vibration and proprioception in the left arm
choices.C: Loss of vibration and proprioception in the right leg
choices.D: Loss of pain and temperature in the right leg
choices.E: Loss of light touch in both arms

rationale: Fasciculus gracilis (medial) carries input from below T6 (lower trunk/leg); fasciculus cuneatus (lateral) is present at/above T6 and carries upper trunk/arm input. Dorsal columns are ipsilateral in the cord, so a left gracilis lesion → left leg deficit.
pearl: Gracilis = Ground (legs, medial); Cuneatus = Ceiling (arms, lateral, at/above T6).

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: Second-order DCML axons ascending in the medial lemniscus terminate on third-order neurons located in which structure?

choices.A: Ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus
choices.D: Ventral lateral (VL) nucleus of the thalamus
choices.E: Ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus

rationale: The medial lemniscus (and spinothalamic tract) carrying body information ends in VPL. VPM (A) receives face information (trigeminothalamic). LGN = vision, MGN = hearing, VL = motor (cerebellum/basal ganglia).
pearl: VPL = Limbs/body; VPM = Mouth/face.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 68-year-old man has a lacunar infarct that eliminates conscious touch, vibration, and position sense from the entire left side of his body, with preserved strength. Third-order fibers were most likely interrupted at which location?

choices.A: Anterior limb of the left internal capsule
choices.B: Genu of the right internal capsule
choices.C: Posterior limb of the right internal capsule

rationale: Third-order axons from VPL travel through the posterior limb of the internal capsule, then the corona radiata, to the postcentral gyrus. A contralateral (left-sided) hemisensory loss implies a right-sided lesion above the medullary decussation. The posterior limb is the "sensory" limb (also carries corticospinal fibers—here a pure sensory lacune may also involve the thalamus).
pearl: Internal capsule = "major highway" compressed between caudate, lentiform nucleus, and thalamus.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 70-year-old woman has an occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery. She has diminished touch and vibration sense in the left foot and leg with relative sparing of the face and arm. Which cortical region is most affected?

choices.A: Lateral postcentral gyrus near the sylvian fissure
choices.B: Posterior part of the paracentral lobule on the medial hemisphere
choices.C: Anterior part of the paracentral lobule only

rationale: The postcentral gyrus does not continue onto the medial surface as a gyrus, but its functional area does: the posterior half of the paracentral lobule represents the leg/foot (sensory); the anterior half is motor. ACA supplies the medial hemisphere. The hand/face occupy the lateral convexity (MCA territory).
pearl: Paracentral lobule: anterior = motor (leg), posterior = sensory (leg). ACA stroke → contralateral leg > arm.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 56-year-old man has a wide-based, stamping gait. He can stand steadily with his eyes open but falls when he closes them. He has absent vibration sense in both feet, absent ankle reflexes, lancinating leg pains, and pupils that accommodate but do not react to light. Which process best explains his deficits?

choices.C: Degeneration of anterior horn motor neurons
choices.D: Demyelination of the lateral corticospinal tracts
choices.E: Demyelination of large fibers in the dorsal roots and dorsal columns from tertiary syphilis

rationale: Tabes dorsalis (tertiary neurosyphilis) damages large-fiber dorsal roots and dorsal columns bilaterally → loss of touch, vibration, and proprioception; positive Romberg (sensory ataxia unmasked by removing visual input); areflexia (afferent limb of the stretch reflex lost); Argyll Robertson pupils.
pearl: Positive Romberg = proprioceptive (dorsal column) deficit, not cerebellar.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of pernicious anemia has paresthesias, loss of vibration and position sense in the legs, spastic weakness, and bilateral Babinski signs. Which combination of spinal cord tracts is most characteristically affected?

choices.A: Dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts
choices.B: Spinothalamic tracts and anterior horn cells only
choices.E: Anterior corticospinal tracts and ventral horns only

rationale: Vitamin B12 deficiency causes subacute combined degeneration: demyelination of the dorsal columns (sensory ataxia, positive Romberg), lateral corticospinal tracts (spastic paresis, hyperreflexia, Babinski), and spinocerebellar tracts (ataxia). Lecture: begins in large fibers of the dorsal columns, then other tracts are affected.
pearl: SCD ("combined" = sensory + motor). Also consider copper deficiency and nitrous oxide abuse (inactivates B12).

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 66-year-old right-handed man can feel a key placed in his left palm (eyes closed) and reports that something is touching him, but he cannot identify the object. He also cannot identify numbers traced on his left palm. Primary touch, vibration, and proprioception are intact. Where is the lesion?

choices.B: Right VPL nucleus of the thalamus
choices.E: Left medial lemniscus in the pons

rationale: Agnosia = loss of a cognitive aspect of sensation despite intact primary sensation. Astereognosis and agraphesthesia result from lesions of the posterior parietal (association) cortex adjacent to the primary somatosensory cortex. Lesions in primary cortex, thalamus, or tracts (A–C, E) cause loss of primary sensation.
pearl: Primary cortex lesion → loss of perception; association cortex lesion → agnosia.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: After a large right-hemisphere stroke, a 72-year-old woman shaves only the right side of her face, eats only food from the right side of her plate, and denies that her left arm belongs to her. Which region is most likely damaged?
rationale: Hemineglect—disregarding the contralateral body and space as if it doesn't exist—typically follows right (nondominant) posterior parietal lesions. Left parietal lesions rarely cause severe neglect because the right hemisphere attends to both hemifields.
pearl: Right parietal → left neglect (± anosognosia, asomatognosia).

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: During a neurologic exam, a 128-Hz tuning fork is placed on the patient's medial malleolus. Which encapsulated, onion-like receptor in the deep dermis and periosteum is primarily responsible for detecting this stimulus?
rationale: Pacinian corpuscles are large, lamellated (onion-skin), rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors located in deep dermis, ligaments, joints, and periosteum—detecting vibration and deep pressure. Free nerve endings (D) carry pain/temperature (ALS).
pearl: Pacinian = Pressure + vibration (deep). Meissner = fine touch (fingertips, superficial).

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: Which receptor, concentrated in the dermal papillae of glabrous (hairless) skin such as the fingertips and lips, is most responsible for fine, discriminative touch such as reading Braille?
rationale: Meissner (tactile) corpuscles are encapsulated, rapidly adapting receptors in the superficial dermis of hairless skin, mediating light/fine discriminative touch and flutter. They are carried in large myelinated Aβ axons in the DCML.
pearl: Fingertips have high receptor density → large cortical representation in the homunculus.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 50-year-old woman has an absent right patellar reflex. Strength in the right quadriceps is normal, and there is numbness over the right medial leg. Interruption of which structure best explains the absent reflex with preserved strength?

choices.A: Right lateral corticospinal tract at T6
choices.E: Right L4 dorsal root (Ia afferents from muscle spindles)

rationale: The stretch reflex is monosynaptic: muscle spindle → Ia afferent (DRG neuron) → short branch synapses on anterior horn α-motor neuron → muscle contraction. The long branch of the same 1st-order axon ascends in the dorsal columns. Interrupting the afferent limb (dorsal root) abolishes the reflex while strength (ventral root, motor neuron) is preserved. The numbness over the medial leg (L4 dermatome) supports an L4 dorsal root lesion.
pearl: Reflex grading 0, 1+, 2+ (normal), 3+, 4+ (clonus). Patellar = L3–L4; Achilles = S1.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A professional violinist undergoes functional imaging. Compared with non-musicians, the cortical representation of the fingers of her left hand in the right postcentral gyrus is markedly enlarged. Which concept best explains this finding?
rationale: The homunculus can change within limits: active cortical areas expand into adjacent unused/underused territory, and use recruits more cortical space. This plasticity underlies skill learning and recovery after brain injury (rewiring circuits).
pearl: "Use reshapes the homunculus." Recovery of function depends on the brain's ability to rewire.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: An MRI shows foraminal stenosis at the intervertebral foramen between the C4 and C5 vertebrae. Which spinal nerve is compressed?
rationale: Spinal nerves C1–C7 exit ABOVE their corresponding vertebrae, so the nerve exiting between C4 and C5 is C5. Because there are 8 cervical nerves but only 7 cervical vertebrae, C8 exits between C7 and T1, and from T1 downward all nerves exit BELOW their vertebrae (the nerve between T1 and T2 is T1).
pearl: Cervical: nerve exits above its vertebra. T1 and below: nerve exits below its vertebra. C8 has no vertebra.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 42-year-old man has a posterolateral disc herniation at L4–L5. Which nerve root is most likely affected, and which finding is expected?

choices.C: S1; numbness of the medial knee
choices.D: L4; numbness over the lateral little toe
choices.E: L5; numbness over the dorsum of the foot and great toe with weak great toe dorsiflexion

rationale: A typical posterolateral lumbar disc herniation affects the next lower spinal nerve (disc L2–L3 affects L3; disc L4–L5 affects L5), because the nerve exiting at that level has already left above the disc. L5: dorsum of foot/great toe sensation, ankle/great toe dorsiflexion (extensor hallucis longus), foot drop. S1: lateral foot/little toe, plantarflexion, Achilles reflex.
pearl: Lumbar disc → hits the lower root (L4–L5 disc → L5).

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 48-year-old woman has neck pain radiating down the lateral forearm into the thumb, with a diminished biceps and brachioradialis reflex. Which dermatome/root is most likely involved?
rationale: C6 dermatome covers the lateral (radial) forearm and thumb; C6 also mediates the biceps/brachioradialis reflexes. C5 = clavicle/shoulder (lateral arm); C7 = middle finger (triceps reflex); C8 = ring and little fingers, medial forearm; T1 = medial arm.
pearl: "Thumbs up = C6 (make a 6 with thumb and index)." C7 index/middle; C8 ring/pinky.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 39-year-old man is stabbed in the back and loses sensation from the level of the nipples downward. Which is the most superior dermatome affected?
rationale: Landmark dermatomes: T4 = nipple line, T6/T7 = xiphoid, T10 = umbilicus, L1 = inguinal ligament.
pearl: "T4 at the teat pore, T10 at the belly butTEN."

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A patient with acute appendicitis initially describes vague periumbilical pain. Visceral afferents from the appendix enter the spinal cord at the same segment that supplies the skin of the umbilicus. Which segment is this?
rationale: The umbilicus is T10. Early appendicitis pain is referred to the T10 dermatome because visceral afferents converge with somatic afferents in the same dorsal horn segment. Pain localizes to McBurney point once the parietal peritoneum is irritated.
pearl: T10 = umbilicus = referred appendix pain.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A lumbar puncture is performed in an adult at the L4–L5 interspace. Why is this level safe?

choices.A: The spinal cord terminates at T12 in all adults
choices.B: The dura terminates at L1, so no CSF is present below that level
choices.C: The conus medullaris ends at about L1–L2; below this the lumbar cistern contains only cauda equina roots, which are displaced by the needle
choices.D: The filum terminale is absent at lumbar levels
choices.E: The epidural space is obliterated below L2

rationale: The cord grows more slowly than the vertebral canal, so in adults the conus medullaris ends at ~L2 (L1–L2). The subarachnoid space continues to S2 as the lumbar cistern, containing CSF and cauda equina roots (L2–Coc1) that float away from the needle. The pia continues as the filum terminale to the coccyx.
pearl: Adult cord ends ~L2; dural sac ends ~S2. LP at L3–L4 or L4–L5 (iliac crests ≈ L4).

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: An anesthesiologist compares epidural anesthesia with spinal anesthesia for a cesarean delivery. Which statement is correct?

choices.A: The epidural space around the brain and spinal cord are both real, fat-filled spaces
choices.B: Epidural anesthesia is injected directly into the CSF of the lumbar cistern
choices.C: Epidural anesthesia produces a faster and more complete block than spinal anesthesia
choices.D: The spinal epidural space is a real space containing fat and veins, allowing catheter infusion for prolonged, segmentally limited block
choices.E: Spinal anesthesia can be safely placed at any vertebral level, including the cervical cord

rationale: In the skull, the epidural space is only a potential space (dura fused to bone) that opens only with an epidural hematoma. In the vertebral canal it is a real space with fat and blood vessels; catheters can infuse anesthetic for long periods with limited diffusion (restricted dermatomal block). Spinal anesthesia (into the lumbar cistern CSF) produces a faster, more complete, but shorter block and must be kept low to avoid affecting cardiac and respiratory function.
pearl: Spinal = subarachnoid (fast, dense, short). Epidural = outside dura (slower, catheter, titratable).

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A histology slide of spinal cord shows a small lateral projection of gray matter between the dorsal and ventral horns. Neurons in this region are best described as which of the following?

choices.A: Lower motor neurons to skeletal muscle of the limbs
choices.B: Preganglionic sympathetic neurons, present from T1 to L2
choices.C: Second-order neurons of the DCML pathway
choices.D: Parasympathetic preganglionic neurons present from C1 to C8

rationale: The lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column) is present at T1–L2(L3) and contains preganglionic sympathetic neurons whose axons exit via the ventral roots. Sacral parasympathetic neurons (S2–S4) are in a similar position but do not form a distinct horn. Its presence identifies a thoracic cross section.
pearl: Dorsal horn = sensory; ventral horn = somatic motor; lateral horn (T1–L2) = sympathetic.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 52-year-old man has severe low back pain after lifting, followed by bilateral leg weakness, numbness of the perineum and inner thighs, decreased ankle reflexes, and urinary retention. Imaging shows a large central disc herniation at L4–L5. Which structure is compressed?

choices.E: Cauda equina nerve roots within the lumbar cistern

rationale: Lesions below L2 affect cauda equina roots (L2–Coc1), producing LMN signs (weakness, hyporeflexia), saddle anesthesia (S2–S5), and bladder/bowel dysfunction. Causes: disc herniation, tumor, infection. It is a neurosurgical emergency.
pearl: Cauda equina = LMN, often asymmetric, radicular pain. Conus medullaris = more symmetric, early bladder dysfunction, mixed UMN/LMN.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 9-year-old girl has progressive scoliosis, low back pain, leg weakness, and new urinary incontinence. Examination shows a lumbosacral hair tuft. MRI shows a low-lying conus medullaris at L4 with a short, thickened filum terminale. What is the diagnosis?

choices.B: Cauda equina syndrome from disc herniation

rationale: In tethered cord syndrome, the conus is abnormally anchored (to subcutaneous tissue, short filum, dural adhesions), preventing normal relative ascent. Traction produces lower body sensory/motor and bladder deficits, back pain, and scoliosis—worsening with growth. Often associated with occult spinal dysraphism (hair tuft, dimple).
pearl: Low-lying conus (below L2) + bladder issues + cutaneous stigmata → tethered cord.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes open repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. Postoperatively he has bilateral leg paralysis, loss of pain and temperature below T10, and urinary retention, but vibration and joint position sense in the legs are intact. Which vessel's compromise explains this?

choices.C: Great anterior segmental artery (of Adamkiewicz) supplying the anterior spinal artery

rationale: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the cord (corticospinal tracts, spinothalamic tracts, anterior horns). The artery of Adamkiewicz is a major contributor for lower thoracic/upper lumbar cord. Dorsal columns are supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries (with robust anastomoses), so vibration/proprioception are spared.
pearl: Anterior spinal artery syndrome: everything lost except dorsal columns.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A spinal cord cross section shows a large oval outline with abundant white matter, prominent ventral horns, a visible fasciculus cuneatus lateral to fasciculus gracilis, and no lateral horn. Which level is this?
rationale: White matter is greatest at cervical levels (all ascending fibers have accumulated and descending fibers have not yet terminated). The cervical enlargement has large ventral horns for upper limb muscles. Fasciculus cuneatus exists only at/above T6. Thoracic: thin horns + lateral horn. Lumbosacral: large gray matter, relatively less white matter; sacral is small and mostly gray.
pearl: White matter decreases cervical → sacral; gray matter largest at enlargements.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: During spinal cord surgery, the neurosurgeon uses a series of about 20 paired, tooth-like lateral attachments as a landmark to separate dorsal from ventral roots. From which meningeal layer do these structures arise?
rationale: Denticulate ligaments are lateral extensions of the pia that pierce the arachnoid and anchor the cord to the dura. They lie between dorsal and ventral roots, dividing the cord into anterior and posterior compartments—a surgical landmark. The pia also continues caudally as the filum terminale.
pearl: Pia → denticulate ligaments + filum terminale. Dura → becomes epineurium of spinal nerves.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A 61-year-old woman develops sudden loss of touch, vibration, and position sense over the entire right side of her body, with left tongue deviation on protrusion and right-sided hemiparesis. Which structure carrying tactile information is damaged?

choices.E: Left medial lemniscus in the medulla

rationale: Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal/vertebral artery branch) affects the medullary pyramid (contralateral hemiparesis), medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of touch/vibration/proprioception—already crossed), and CN XII (ipsilateral tongue deviation toward the lesion). Left tongue deviation → left lesion → right body deficits.
pearl: Once DCML axons decussate (caudal medulla), lesions produce contralateral deficits.

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A lecturer states that an action potential travelling 1 meter from the finger to the spinal cord takes about 8 ms in the fastest axon but ~100 ms in the slowest mechanoreceptor axon. Which property most determines this difference?

choices.A: The number of synapses along the axon
choices.B: The modality of the stimulus only
choices.C: The distance between receptor and DRG
choices.D: Axon diameter and degree of myelination

rationale: Larger diameter (lower internal resistance) and thicker myelin (saltatory conduction) increase conduction velocity. Different sensory systems use different axon sizes: DCML tactile/proprioceptive information travels in large myelinated Aα/Aβ fibers; pain/temperature in thin Aδ and unmyelinated C fibers. Axon size also determines differential vulnerability to disease (e.g., large-fiber neuropathies).
pearl: Aα (proprioception, Ia) > Aβ (touch/vibration) > Aδ (fast pain/cold) > C (slow pain/warmth).

lecture: 2.1 Tactile Sensory Pathway (DCML) & Spinal Cord (Dr. Freedman / Dr. Cohan)
stem: A patient has a lesion causing loss of touch and proprioception from the left side of the body. Which lesion location would produce this deficit?

choices.B: Right VPL nucleus of the thalamus
choices.D: Right dorsal root ganglion at T2
choices.E: Left posterior limb of the internal capsule

rationale: Because DCML fibers decussate in the caudal medulla, lesions above the medulla (medial lemniscus, VPL, internal capsule, postcentral gyrus) cause contralateral deficits; lesions in the cord, dorsal roots, or DRG cause ipsilateral deficits. Left-sided body loss → right thalamus/capsule/cortex, or left cord/root. Only B fits.
pearl: Symptoms are always reported where the stimulus arose—localize by level relative to the decussation.

stem: A 40-year-old soldier sustains a severe leg wound in combat but reports minimal pain until he reaches safety hours later. Conversely, a 35-year-old woman reports severe pain in an amputated limb. These observations best illustrate which concept?

choices.A: Pain intensity is directly proportional to nociceptor firing rate
choices.B: Nociception and pain are identical processes
choices.C: Pain can only arise from stimulation of peripheral nociceptors
choices.D: Pain is a subjective biopsychosocial experience that can occur without nociceptor stimulation and vary with context
choices.E: Fast pain fibers are blocked by stress hormones

rationale: Nociception is the detection and localization of a stimulated pain receptor; pain is the complex, subjective sensory and emotional experience. Pain can arise without nociceptor activation (phantom limb) and the same stimulus can be very painful in one context and almost painless in another (attention, emotion, environment). Encoding does not guarantee perception.
pearl: Pain = nociception + psychological/emotional factors + environment.

stem: A man steps on a tack and immediately feels a sharp, well-localized pain before withdrawing his foot. Which fiber type and pathway carry this "first pain"?

choices.A: C fibers in the spino-reticulo-thalamic tract to the insula
choices.B: Aδ fibers in the spinothalamic tract to VPL and the postcentral gyrus
choices.C: Aβ fibers in the dorsal columns to the nucleus gracilis
choices.D: Aα fibers in the dorsal spinocerebellar tract
choices.E: C fibers in the dorsal columns to VPM

rationale: Fast pain is carried by thinly myelinated Aδ fibers in the spinothalamic tract → VPL → postcentral gyrus. It is sensory-discriminative (location, intensity, onset, duration) and is the pathway used for lesion localization (pin-prick testing).
pearl: First pain: Aδ, sharp, localized, spinothalamic. Second pain: C, burning/aching, spino-reticulo-thalamic.

stem: Several seconds after burning his hand on a stove, a cook experiences a prolonged, poorly localized, burning, throbbing pain that persists after the stimulus ends and is worsened by anxiety. Which structures mediate the unpleasant affective quality of this pain?

choices.A: Aβ fibers → nucleus cuneatus → primary somatosensory cortex
choices.B: Aδ fibers → marginal zone → postcentral gyrus
choices.C: Ia afferents → anterior horn motor neurons
choices.E: C fibers → substantia gelatinosa → spino-reticulo-thalamic tract → anterior cingulate gyrus and insula

rationale: Slow pain uses the smallest, unmyelinated C fibers synapsing in the substantia gelatinosa (lamina II), with a multisynaptic route through the brainstem reticular formation to different thalamic nuclei, then to the anterior cingulate gyrus and insula (emotional "disturbing" quality). It is not used for localization and is the major target for drug therapy.
pearl: Slow pain → cingulate + insula = "how much it bothers you."

stem: As the central processes of first-order pain and temperature neurons enter the spinal cord, they travel briefly in which tract before entering the dorsal horn?
rationale: First-order ALS axons (DRG cell bodies) enter via the dorsal root, travel up or down 1–2 segments in the dorsolateral fasciculus (Lissauer tract), then synapse ipsilaterally in the dorsal horn (marginal zone, lamina I; nucleus proprius; substantia gelatinosa for slow pain).
pearl: ALS 1° → Lissauer tract → dorsal horn (ipsilateral). 2° crosses in anterior white commissure.

stem: Second-order neurons of the spinothalamic tract cross the midline at which location?

choices.A: Caudal medulla via the internal arcuate fibers
choices.C: Anterior white commissure of the spinal cord, near the level of entry

rationale: Second-order axons from the marginal zone and nucleus proprius cross in the anterior white commissure, rising rostrally ~2 segments as they cross, then ascend contralaterally in the ALS. Contrast with DCML (crosses in caudal medulla via internal arcuate fibers) and corticospinal (pyramidal decussation).
pearl: Pain crosses early (cord); touch crosses late (medulla).

stem: A tumor compresses only the right anterolateral system at the C7 cord level. What sensory deficit results?

choices.A: Loss of pain and temperature on the right side below C7
choices.B: Loss of vibration on the right side below C7
choices.C: Bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a cape distribution
choices.D: Loss of pain and temperature on the left side from C7 upward
choices.E: Loss of pain and temperature on the left side beginning about 2 segments below the lesion (~T1) and downward

rationale: The ALS carries pain/temperature from the opposite side (fibers already crossed). Because second-order axons ascend ~2 segments while crossing, a lesion in the ALS produces contralateral loss beginning about 2 levels below the lesion and continuing through the rest of the body. Dorsal columns are spared.
pearl: ALS lesion → contralateral P&T loss starting ~2 segments below.

stem: A 30-year-old man with a history of Chiari I malformation has burns on his hands he did not notice. Examination shows bilateral loss of pain and temperature over the shoulders, arms, and upper back with preserved vibration and proprioception. Later, hand muscle wasting develops. What is the mechanism of the sensory loss?

choices.A: Expansion of a central cavity compressing crossing fibers in the anterior white commissure
choices.B: Compression of the dorsal columns by a posterior disc
choices.C: Occlusion of the posterior spinal arteries
choices.D: Demyelination of the dorsal roots by Treponema pallidum

rationale: Syringomyelia (syrinx, often cervical, associated with Chiari I) compresses the anterior white commissure first → bilateral, segmental "cape-like" loss of pain/temperature with preserved dorsal column function (dissociated sensory loss). Expansion into the anterior horns causes LMN signs (hand atrophy); into the lateral corticospinal tracts causes UMN signs.
pearl: Cape-like bilateral P&T loss + preserved vibration = syringomyelia.

stem: A 28-year-old man is stabbed in the back, hemisecting the right side of his spinal cord at T8. Which pattern of sensory loss is expected?

choices.A: Bilateral loss of all sensation below T8
choices.B: Left loss of vibration and right loss of pain/temperature below T8
choices.C: Right loss of vibration/proprioception below T8 and left loss of pain/temperature beginning ~T10
choices.D: Right loss of pain/temperature only, at the T8 dermatome
choices.E: Left loss of vibration and pain/temperature below T8
