Which intervertebral disc space is most likely herniated, and which exiting/traversing nerve root is compressed?
rationale: Posterolateral disc herniation at the L5–S1 interspace typically compresses the traversing S1 nerve root. S1 radiculopathy produces: (1) sensory loss/pain along the posterior thigh, posterior calf, lateral border of the foot, and sole; (2) motor weakness of gastrocnemius/soleus (impaired plantarflexion, inability to toe-walk); and (3) diminished or absent Achilles tendon deep tendon reflex (S1–S2). In contrast, an L4–L5 herniation compresses the traversing L5 root (weakness of dorsiflexion, difficulty heel-walking, intact reflexes).
pearl: L5–S1 disc herniation compresses S1 root: Weak plantarflexion (difficulty toe-walking), absent Achilles reflex, numbness of lateral foot/sole.

stem: A 54-year-old woman is evaluated in the neurology clinic for progressive sensory deficits. On examination, she exhibits profound loss of two-point discrimination, vibration, and conscious joint position sense involving the entire right arm, forearm, and hand, continuing down the right trunk and right lower extremity. Sensation on the left side of her body is entirely normal. Pinprick, sharp pain, and temperature sensation are completely preserved on both sides of her body, and motor strength is 5/5 bilaterally. Where is the most likely neuroanatomical location of this lesion?

choices.A: Right dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) in the high cervical spinal cord (C1–C2)
choices.B: Left primary somatosensory cortex postcentral gyrus
choices.C: Left medial lemniscus in the mid-pons
choices.D: Right ventral white commissure across C5–T1
choices.E: Left ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus

rationale: The patient has an isolated, unilateral loss of DCML modalities (light touch, vibration, proprioception) encompassing the entire right upper extremity, trunk, and lower extremity, with complete sparing of pain/temperature and motor function. Because the deficit involves the arm, trunk, and leg on the *ipsilateral* side, the lesion must be located in the uncrossed first-order dorsal columns of the spinal cord above the C5 level (i.e., at C1–C2), where both fasciculus gracilis (leg) and fasciculus cuneatus (arm) are present on the right side. Above the caudal medulla, DCML fibers decussate as internal arcuate fibers, so a brainstem (medial lemniscus), thalamic (VPL), or cortical lesion would produce *contralateral* sensory loss.
pearl: Ipsilateral loss of vibration/proprioception across the entire arm and leg indicates an ipsilateral dorsal column lesion in the high cervical cord (above C5) or caudal medulla prior to decussation.

stem: A 43-year-old carpenter presents with shooting pain and numbness over his right shoulder and lateral arm, radiating down the radial forearm into the thumb. Physical examination reveals reduced light touch and pinprick sensation strictly over the thumb and lateral aspect of the forearm on the right side. Biceps deep tendon reflex is 1+ on the right and 2+ on the left. Triceps and brachioradialis reflexes are normal. Motor examination shows 4/5 strength in right elbow flexion and wrist extension. What is the most likely location and nature of this lesion?

choices.A: Right radial nerve entrapment at the spiral groove
choices.B: Right C6 spinal nerve root compression (radiculopathy)
choices.C: Right median nerve compression at the pronator teres
choices.D: Left lateral spinothalamic tract at C4
choices.E: Right posterior cord of the brachial plexus

rationale: The patient exhibits classic signs of a C6 radiculopathy: (1) sensory loss/pain in the C6 dermatome (lateral arm, lateral forearm, and digit 1/thumb); (2) motor weakness in C6 myotomes (biceps elbow flexion and wrist extension); and (3) diminished biceps reflex (C5–C6). A peripheral radial nerve entrapment would spare elbow flexion (innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve) and would not produce isolated thumb dermatomal loss with biceps reflex reduction.
pearl: C6 radiculopathy: Pain/numbness radiating to the thumb (digit 1) and radial forearm, weakness of wrist extension and elbow flexion, diminished biceps reflex.

stem: A 38-year-old dental hygienist presents with nocturnal burning pain and paresthesias in her right hand that frequently awaken her from sleep. On examination, sensation to light touch and pinprick is diminished over the palmar surface of the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and the lateral half of the ring finger. Sensation over the thenar eminence of the palm is completely intact. Phalen test and Tinel sign at the volar wrist are positive. What anatomical feature explains why sensation over the thenar eminence is spared in this patient?

choices.A: The thenar eminence is innervated exclusively by the superficial radial nerve
choices.B: The C8 nerve root supplies sensory innervation to the central palm
choices.C: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve arises proximal to the flexor retinaculum and passes superficial to the carpal tunnel
choices.D: Thenar skin is innervated by sympathetic fibers from the stellate ganglion
choices.E: Ulnar nerve collateral branches cross the midpalmar raphe to supply the entire palm

rationale: This patient has Carpal Tunnel Syndrome (median nerve entrapment under the transverse carpal ligament / flexor retinaculum). The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve provides sensation to the skin of the thenar eminence. Crucially, this branch arises approximately 5 cm *proximal* to the wrist crease and passes *superficial* to the flexor retinaculum (outside the carpal tunnel). Therefore, carpal tunnel compression compromises only the digital branches traveling *through* the tunnel (digits 1, 2, 3, and lateral 4), completely sparing sensation over the thenar eminence. Sensation loss over the thenar eminence suggests a proximal lesion (e.g., C6 radiculopathy or pronator teres syndrome).
pearl: In carpal tunnel syndrome, sensation over the thenar eminence is *spared* because the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to (outside) the flexor retinaculum.

stem: A clinical neurologist compares three patients presenting with upper extremity sensory symptoms: Patient 1 has numbness restricted to the palmar aspect of the first three and a half digits (peripheral nerve distribution); Patient 2 has numbness radiating down the lateral forearm into the thumb (dermatomal distribution); and Patient 3 has loss of touch and vibration across the entire arm and leg on one side (funicular/tract distribution). Which of the following rules is most reliable for distinguishing a single peripheral nerve lesion from a spinal nerve root (radiculopathy) lesion in the clinic?

choices.A: Radiculopathies never cause pain, whereas peripheral nerve injuries are always painful
choices.B: Peripheral nerve lesions always affect deep tendon reflexes, whereas radiculopathies never alter reflexes
choices.C: Radiculopathies produce spasticity and hyperreflexia, while peripheral nerves produce flaccidity
choices.D: Peripheral nerve lesions produce sensory loss that conforms strictly to the anatomical branching field of an individual named nerve (often overlapping multiple spinal roots), whereas radiculopathies produce sensory loss conforming to a continuous dermatomal strip
choices.E: Peripheral nerve lesions always cross the midline of the body

rationale: Distinguishing peripheral nerve vs. root vs. tract lesions relies on anatomical mapping: (1) Peripheral nerve lesions (e.g., median nerve, ulnar nerve) affect sensory territories defined by the terminal cutaneous branch of that specific nerve, which is derived from multiple spinal cord levels (e.g., median nerve contains C6–T1 fibers); (2) Radiculopathies (e.g., C6, C7) affect a continuous dermatomal strip corresponding to a single embryological spinal segment; (3) Tract/spinal cord lesions (e.g., dorsal column, ALS) produce sensory deficits across all body regions below the level of the lesion (funicular distribution).
pearl: Peripheral nerve lesion = territory of a named nerve (multi-root origin); Radiculopathy = dermatomal strip corresponding to a single spinal root.

stem: A 49-year-old warehouse supervisor experiences sudden, severe electric-shock pain shooting from his left lower back down the posterior thigh, posterior calf, and into the lateral border of his foot and small toe after lifting a heavy crate. Physical examination reveals decreased sensation over the lateral margin of the left foot and sole, weakness when attempting to walk on his left toes (impaired plantarflexion), and a completely absent left Achilles tendon reflex. The patellar reflex is 2+ bilaterally. What diagnosis and spinal nerve root are implicated?

choices.A: Meralgia paresthetica; Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve

rationale: The patient has acute sciatica due to an S1 radiculopathy (commonly caused by an L5–S1 posterolateral disc herniation compressing the traversing S1 root). The clinical triad of S1 radiculopathy is: (1) sensory loss/pain down the posterior leg to the lateral foot/sole/fifth toe; (2) weakness of plantarflexion (gastrocnemius/soleus), causing difficulty with toe-walking; and (3) diminished or absent Achilles tendon deep tendon reflex (mediated by S1–S2).
pearl: S1 radiculopathy: Pain radiating to the lateral foot and small toe, weak plantarflexion (cannot toe-walk), absent Achilles reflex.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive tingling, numbness, and burning dysesthesias in his feet and lower legs over the past 3 months. Nerve conduction studies (NCS) performed along the tibial and peroneal nerves demonstrate a 45% reduction in motor and sensory nerve conduction velocity (NCV) along with marked prolongation of distal latencies. Needle electromyography shows no spontaneous fibrillations at rest. What pathological alteration in the peripheral nervous system is directly responsible for the slowed conduction velocity?

choices.A: Demyelination of peripheral nerve fibers with loss of saltatory conduction
choices.B: Primary axonal transection with Wallerian degeneration
choices.C: Complete necrosis of anterior horn alpha motor neurons
choices.D: Destruction of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction

rationale: Nerve conduction velocity (NCV) depends directly on the integrity of the myelin sheath produced by Schwann cells. In demyelinating polyneuropathies (such as chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, CIDP, or Guillain-Barré syndrome), loss of myelin increases membrane capacitance and decreases transverse membrane resistance, causing electrotonic currents to dissipate through the demyelinated axolemma. This prevents rapid saltatory conduction from node to node, resulting in markedly reduced NCV and prolonged distal onset latencies. In contrast, pure axonal loss causes decreased amplitude with preserved velocity.
pearl: Slowed nerve conduction velocity (NCV) and prolonged latencies on NCS are the definitive hallmarks of demyelinating neuropathy (loss of saltatory conduction).

stem: A 46-year-old man presents with right lower extremity pain and numbness. Neurological examination reveals marked weakness of right ankle dorsiflexion and great toe extension. When asked to walk across the room on his heels, he is unable to do so on the right side and his foot slaps down (foot drop). However, he can walk on his toes without difficulty. Sensation to pinprick is diminished over the anterolateral leg and the dorsum of the right foot including the great toe. Both patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes are 2+ and symmetric. An MRI confirms a posterolateral intervertebral disc herniation. Between which vertebral bodies is the herniation located, and which nerve root is compressed?
rationale: The patient has an L5 radiculopathy, typically caused by a posterolateral disc herniation at the L4–L5 intervertebral space compressing the traversing L5 nerve root. The hallmark findings of L5 radiculopathy are: (1) sensory loss across the anterolateral lower leg, dorsum of the foot, and great toe (hallux); (2) motor weakness of ankle dorsiflexion (tibialis anterior) and toe extension (extensor hallucis longus), resulting in difficulty heel-walking and foot drop; and (3) *intact* reflexes, because there is no readily testable deep tendon reflex mediated primarily by L5 (patellar is L2–L4; Achilles is S1–S2).
pearl: L4–L5 disc herniation compresses L5 root: Foot drop, weak dorsiflexion (cannot heel-walk), sensory loss on dorsum of foot/big toe, *normal* patellar and Achilles reflexes.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents with severe anterior thigh and medial leg pain. On examination, she has weakness of knee extension (quadriceps) and difficulty standing up from a seated position or squatting. Sensation is decreased over the anterior lower thigh, patella, and down the medial malleolus of the ankle. The right patellar tendon reflex is absent, while the Achilles reflex is normal. A lumbar spine MRI demonstrates a disc herniation. At which level is the disc herniation, and which nerve root is compressed?
rationale: The patient presents with an L4 radiculopathy, commonly caused by a posterolateral disc herniation at the L3–L4 intervertebral space compressing the traversing L4 root. The clinical features of L4 radiculopathy are: (1) pain and sensory loss over the anterior thigh, anterior knee, and down the medial lower leg to the medial malleolus; (2) motor weakness of knee extension (quadriceps femoris); and (3) diminished or absent patellar tendon reflex (knee jerk, L2–L4, predominantly L4).
pearl: L3–L4 disc herniation compresses L4 root: Quadriceps weakness (impaired knee extension/squatting), absent patellar reflex, numbness over medial malleolus.

stem: A 30-year-old competitive cyclist presents with numbness and paresthesias involving the fourth and fifth digits of his left hand and weakness of finger abduction. Physical examination reveals sensory loss over the hypothenar eminence and the medial one and a half digits. Finger abduction against resistance (dorsal interossei) is 3/5. Froment sign is positive in the left hand. Sensation over the thenar eminence, lateral palm, and thumb is completely normal. Which peripheral nerve is entrapped in this patient?

choices.A: Median nerve at the pronator teres
choices.B: Radial nerve at the arcade of Frohse
choices.D: Ulnar nerve at Guyon canal (or cubital tunnel)
choices.E: Axillary nerve in the quadrangular space

rationale: The patient has ulnar neuropathy (often called "cyclist\'s palsy" due to compression of the ulnar nerve against handlebars at Guyon canal at the wrist, or at the cubital tunnel of the elbow). The ulnar nerve innervates: (1) sensation to the hypothenar eminence, small finger, and medial half of the ring finger; and (2) motor supply to intrinsic hand muscles, including the dorsal interossei (finger abduction) and adductor pollicis. Weakness of adductor pollicis produces a positive Froment sign (compensatory flexion of the thumb interphalangeal joint by the median-innervated flexor pollicis longus when pinching a piece of paper).
pearl: Ulnar nerve entrapment (Guyon canal / cubital tunnel): Sensory loss over digit 5 and medial digit 4, weak finger abduction (interossei), positive Froment sign.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents with chronic lower back pain and leg fatigue that worsens after walking two blocks and improves when he bends forward or leans over a shopping cart ("shopping cart sign"). Physical examination shows normal pedal pulses and no focal sensory or motor deficits at rest. Lumbar MRI reveals diffuse osteophyte formation, ligamentum flavum hypertrophy, and degenerative disc bulging resulting in severe narrowing of the central spinal canal from L2 through L5. What is this clinical syndrome called?
rationale: Lumbar spinal stenosis leads to neurogenic claudication (pseudoclaudication). Hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, facet joint arthropathy, and degenerative disc disease narrow the central spinal canal, compressing the cauda equina and its microvasculature. Symptoms include bilateral buttocks/thigh/calf pain, numbness, and cramping brought on by walking or standing (spinal extension narrows the canal further). Leaning forward (flexion of the spine, as over a shopping cart) increases the canal diameter and decompresses the nerve roots, providing rapid relief. Normal pulses distinguish it from vascular claudication.
pearl: Neurogenic claudication (spinal stenosis): Pain/numbness provoked by walking and spinal extension, relieved by spinal flexion ("shopping cart sign").

stem: A 27-year-old man is stabbed in the back during an altercation. Neurological examination reveals a spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Séquard syndrome) at the T8 level on the right side. Which of the following sensory and motor profiles will be present below the level of the lesion?

choices.A: Right-sided spastic paralysis and loss of vibration/proprioception; Left-sided loss of pain and temperature
choices.B: Left-sided spastic paralysis and loss of vibration/proprioception; Right-sided loss of pain and temperature
choices.C: Bilateral loss of pain and temperature with complete preservation of motor function
choices.D: Right-sided loss of pain and temperature with bilateral flaccid paraplegia
choices.E: Complete anesthesia of both lower extremities with intact upper extremity reflexes

rationale: In Brown-Séquard syndrome (spinal cord hemisection), three primary pathways are severed: (1) Lateral corticospinal tract: severed above lower motor neurons, causing *ipsilateral* upper motor neuron paralysis and spasticity below the lesion; (2) Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis): uncrossed in the spinal cord, causing *ipsilateral* loss of vibration, joint position sense, and discriminative touch below the lesion; (3) Anterolateral system (spinothalamic tract): carries crossed pain and temperature fibers that decussated below the lesion, causing *contralateral* loss of pain and temperature beginning 1–2 segments below the lesion level.
pearl: Brown-Séquard (hemisection): *Ipsilateral* UMN weakness and loss of DCML (proprioception/vibration); *Contralateral* loss of ALS (pain and temperature).

stem: A 72-year-old woman undergoes endovascular repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. Postoperatively, she develops flaccid paralysis of both lower extremities, urinary retention, and bilateral loss of pinprick and temperature sensation below the T10 dermatome. In contrast, vibration perception and joint position sense remain completely intact in both feet. Occlusion of which critical radicular feeding vessel during aortic cross-clamping resulted in this anterior spinal cord syndrome?

choices.B: Great anterior radicular artery of Adamkiewicz

rationale: The patient has Anterior Spinal Artery (ASA) syndrome, an ischemic infarction of the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. The single ASA is reinforced in the lower thoracic and lumbar regions by the Artery of Adamkiewicz (great anterior radicular artery), which typically arises from a left intercostal or lumbar artery between T9 and T12. Cross-clamping or surgical repair of the thoracoabdominal aorta can sacrifice this artery, leading to anterior cord ischemia. The anterior 2/3 of the cord contains the lateral corticospinal tracts (bilateral paralysis) and spinothalamic tracts (bilateral loss of pain/temp). The posterior 1/3 (dorsal columns) is supplied by paired posterior spinal arteries (PSAs) and is completely spared (intact vibration/proprioception).
pearl: Artery of Adamkiewicz supplies the anterior 2/3 of the lower spinal cord. Occlusion causes ASA syndrome: Bilateral paralysis and loss of pain/temp, with *spared dorsal columns*.

stem: A 35-year-old software developer complains of progressive aching in the radial aspect of her right forearm and weakness of finger and thumb extension. Sensory testing reveals normal light touch across the entire hand and arm, with NO cutaneous sensory loss anywhere. On motor exam, she cannot extend her metacarpophalangeal joints, but wrist extension is preserved with slight radial deviation. Where is the nerve entrapment located?

choices.A: Median nerve under the bicipital aponeurosis
choices.B: Ulnar nerve in the canal of Guyon
choices.C: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve) at the arcade of Frohse
choices.D: Musculocutaneous nerve at the lateral antebrachial cutaneous branch
choices.E: Axillary nerve at the humeroscapular groove

rationale: The radial nerve divides in the proximal forearm into a superficial branch (purely sensory to the dorsolateral hand) and a deep motor branch. The deep branch pierces the supinator muscle through a fibrous arch (the arcade of Frohse), where it becomes the Posterior Interosseous Nerve (PIN). Entrapment of the PIN produces pure motor weakness of finger and thumb extension (extensor digitorum, extensor pollicis longus/brevis) with *absolutely no sensory loss*. Wrist extension is preserved (supplied by the radial nerve proper to the extensor carpi radialis longus proximal to the supinator), but shows radial deviation.
pearl: Posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) syndrome = Pure motor weakness of finger/thumb extension with *no sensory deficit* (entrapped at the arcade of Frohse).

stem: A 44-year-old woman presents with bilateral burning hand pain and loss of pain perception in her fingers. Neurological examination reveals cape-like analgesia and thermanesthesia from C4 to T2 bilaterally, with intact light touch. In addition, she has atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of both hands and bilateral loss of the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes. An MRI confirms a large cervical syrinx. What anatomical extension of the syrinx accounts for the muscle wasting and hyporeflexia in this patient?

choices.A: Lateral funiculus compression destroying corticospinal axons
choices.B: Caudal expansion into the lumbar cistern compressing cauda equina
choices.C: Dorsal root ganglion compression outside the spine
choices.D: Lateral expansion of the cavity into the anterior (ventral) horns of the cervical spinal cord
choices.E: Cranial migration into the fourth ventricle obstructing CSF

rationale: As syringomyelia progresses, the expanding cavity within the central cord can extend laterally from the central canal into the anterior (ventral) horns of the gray matter. The ventral horns contain the cell bodies of somatic lower motor neurons (alpha motor neurons). Destruction of these anterior horn cells at the C5–T1 cervical levels produces lower motor neuron signs in the upper extremities: flaccid weakness, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and loss of deep tendon reflexes (biceps, brachioradialis) at the level of the lesion.
pearl: Advanced syringomyelia: Expansion into anterior horns causes *lower motor neuron signs* (hand muscle atrophy, weakness, areflexia) in addition to cape-like pain/temp loss.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with severe tingling and numbness in her right hand digits 1–3. An electrodiagnostic medicine specialist performs a nerve conduction study (NCS). Stimulation of the right median nerve at the wrist produces an onset latency of 5.2 ms (normal < 3.5 ms) when recording from the abductor pollicis brevis, but the compound muscle action potential amplitude is preserved at 9.0 mV. Which of the following best characterizes this electrodiagnostic abnormality?

choices.A: Complete axonal transection with secondary Wallerian degeneration
choices.B: Severe anterior horn motor neuron cell death
choices.E: Focal demyelination causing prolonged distal motor latency

rationale: In focal entrapment neuropathies like Carpal Tunnel Syndrome, mechanical compression and local ischemia lead to focal demyelination of the median nerve as it traverses the flexor retinaculum. Demyelination slows conduction across the compressed segment, which manifests on NCS as a markedly prolonged distal motor latency (5.2 ms vs normal < 3.5 ms) and prolonged sensory latency. Because axons have not degenerated, the compound muscle action potential (CMAP) amplitude remains robust (9.0 mV).
pearl: Carpal tunnel electrodiagnosis: Prolonged distal motor/sensory latency due to focal demyelination under the flexor retinaculum, with preserved amplitude in early disease.

stem: A 29-year-old marathon runner presents with deep aching in the sole of his left foot, accompanied by burning paresthesias radiating to the plantar surfaces of his toes. The pain is exacerbated by prolonged standing and running. Physical examination reveals tenderness posterior and inferior to the medial malleolus, where percussion reproduces tingling in the sole (positive Tinel sign). Sensation is diminished over the plantar surface of the foot, but sensation over the dorsum of the foot is completely normal. What nerve is compressed, and in what anatomical tunnel?

choices.A: Tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel
choices.B: Deep fibular nerve in the anterior tarsal tunnel
choices.C: Superficial fibular nerve in the lateral compartment
choices.D: Sural nerve in the retromalleolar groove
choices.E: Saphenous nerve in the adductor canal

rationale: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is an entrapment neuropathy of the tibial nerve (or its terminal branches, the medial and lateral plantar nerves) as it passes behind and beneath the medial malleolus within the fibro-osseous tarsal tunnel beneath the flexor retinaculum. Clinical features include burning pain, paresthesias, and numbness over the sole of the foot and plantar surfaces of the toes, with a positive Tinel sign behind the medial malleolus. Sensation over the dorsum of the foot is spared because it is supplied by the superficial and deep fibular (peroneal) nerves.
pearl: Tarsal tunnel syndrome = Tibial nerve entrapment behind the medial malleolus; burning sole pain, positive Tinel sign behind medial malleolus, normal dorsal foot sensation.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with chronic lower extremity pain and numbness. Sensory testing reveals loss of pinprick and temperature sensation in a stocking-grasp distribution bilaterally, with reduced vibration perception at the toes. Ankle reflexes are absent. Nerve biopsy demonstrates extensive loss of unmyelinated and small myelinated axons with microvascular hyalinization of endoneurial arterioles. What is the most common underlying etiology of this distal symmetric polyneuropathy worldwide?
rationale: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the most frequent cause of distal symmetric polyneuropathy worldwide. Chronic hyperglycemia leads to microvascular sorbitol accumulation, advanced glycation end-products (AGEs), and endoneurial arteriole microangiopathy, resulting in ischemic and metabolic axonal degeneration. It presents in a length-dependent "stocking-glove" distribution, beginning in the distal lower extremities and slowly progressing proximally. Small-fiber involvement causes burning pain and loss of temperature/pinprick; large-fiber involvement causes loss of vibration, proprioception, and absent Achilles reflexes.
pearl: Diabetic neuropathy = Distal symmetric, length-dependent ("stocking-glove") sensorimotor axonal polyneuropathy from microvascular and metabolic injury.

stem: A 40-year-old woman is evaluated for right arm weakness. She has a complete foot drop and sensory loss over the dorsum of the left foot, and two weeks later develops right wrist drop and sensory loss over the first dorsal web space of the right hand. Workup reveals systemic necrotizing vasculitis (polyarteritis nodosa). What is the clinical neurological term for asymmetric, asynchronous, sequential damage to two or more individual named peripheral nerves?
rationale: Mononeuropathy multiplex (mononeuritis multiplex) refers to simultaneous or sequential, asymmetric, patchy involvement of two or more non-contiguous, distinct peripheral nerves (e.g., right radial nerve plus left common fibular nerve). It is the classic neurological manifestation of systemic vasculitis (such as polyarteritis nodosa, microscopic polyangiitis, or eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis / Churg-Strauss), caused by ischemic infarction of individual nerves due to occlusion of the vasa nervorum.
pearl: Mononeuropathy multiplex = Asymmetric, asynchronous involvement of multiple named individual nerves; classic presentation of vasculitis (ischemic infarction of vasa nervorum).

stem: A 33-year-old construction worker presents with low back pain radiating down the posterior aspect of his right leg into his lateral foot. Straight leg raise (Lasègue test) is positive on the right at 35 degrees, reproducing the shooting radicular pain below the knee. In addition, when the examiner raises the patient\'s UNINVOLVED left leg, the patient reports intense shooting pain radiating down the INVOLVED right leg (crossed straight leg raise sign). What does the crossed straight leg raise sign specifically indicate?

choices.C: Spasticity of the contralateral gastrocnemius muscle
choices.D: High specificity for a herniated intervertebral disc with nerve root compression

rationale: The straight leg raise (SLR) test stretches the sciatic nerve and L5/S1 nerve roots. While a positive ipsilateral SLR is sensitive (~90%) for lumbar disc herniation, it has relatively low specificity (~40%). In contrast, the crossed straight leg raise test (pain reproduced in the symptomatic leg when lifting the *contralateral, asymptomatic* leg) is exceptionally specific (>90%) for a severe herniated intervertebral disc with significant nerve root impingement.
pearl: Crossed straight leg raise test (pain in the affected leg when raising the unaffected leg) has >90% specificity for lumbar disc herniation with nerve root compression.

stem: A 68-year-old woman with a history of breast cancer presents with progressive numbness in her legs. Neurological examination reveals a sensory level to pinprick at the T10 dermatome (umbilicus), bilateral hyperreflexia in the lower extremities, and bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski signs). Upper extremity strength and sensation are completely normal. Emergency spinal MRI demonstrates a metastatic extradural mass compressing the spinal cord at T8. What clinical syndrome is this patient demonstrating?
rationale: Acute spinal cord compression (compressive myelopathy) is an oncologic and neurological emergency. Compression of the thoracic spinal cord produces: (1) a distinct sensory level to pinprick (e.g., T10 dermatome at the umbilicus), below which pain, temperature, and touch sensations are diminished; (2) bilateral upper motor neuron signs below the level of the lesion (spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, bilateral extensor plantar/Babinski responses); and (3) autonomic bladder/bowel dysfunction. Emergent high-dose corticosteroids (dexamethasone) and surgical decompression/radiation are required to prevent permanent paraplegia.
pearl: Compressive myelopathy: Distinct dermatomal sensory level + bilateral UMN signs below the lesion; requires emergent dexamethasone and MRI to prevent paraplegia.

stem: A 63-year-old man presents with acute onset of right-sided hemiparesis and contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception, with sparing of the face. An MRI demonstrates an acute ischemic infarct in the ventromedial medulla (Dejerine anterior bulbar syndrome) caused by occlusion of the anterior spinal artery. On a transverse histological cross-section through the open rostral medulla, which structure lies immediately dorsal to the medullary pyramids in the paramedian region and transmits conscious proprioception and discriminative touch from the contralateral body?
rationale: In the medulla oblongata, the medial lemniscus is oriented vertically in the paramedian zone, positioned immediately dorsal to the medullary pyramids and medial to the inferior olivary nucleus. It carries crossed second-order tactile, vibratory, and proprioceptive fibers ascending from the contralateral nucleus gracilis and cuneatus toward the thalamus. Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery or paramedian branches of the vertebral artery causes medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome), damaging the pyramid (contralateral hemiparesis), the hypoglossal nerve (ipsilateral tongue deviation), and the medial lemniscus (contralateral loss of touch and proprioception).
pearl: Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal artery infarct): Triad of contralateral hemiparesis (pyramid), contralateral loss of vibration/proprioception (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue deviation (CN XII).

stem: An axial myelin-stained cross-section of the thoracic spinal cord at the T10 level is evaluated. A pathologist points to the dorsal funiculus immediately adjacent to the posterior median sulcus. Which specific white matter bundle occupies this medial position in the dorsal column, and from which spinal cord levels does it carry tactile information?

choices.A: Fasciculus cuneatus carrying inputs from C1 to C8
choices.B: Fasciculus gracilis carrying inputs from T6 and below (lower trunk and lower extremities)
choices.C: Lateral spinothalamic tract carrying pain from the contralateral arm
choices.D: Dorsolateral tract of Lissauer carrying unmyelinated preganglionic fibers
choices.E: Anterior corticospinal tract carrying motor fibers to the axial musculature

rationale: The dorsal columns are divided somatotopically: the medial bundle is the fasciculus gracilis, which carries conscious proprioception, two-point discrimination, and vibration from spinal levels T6 and below (sacral, lumbar, and lower thoracic levels, corresponding to the lower extremities and lower trunk). Because the upper extremity fibers have not yet entered the spinal cord at T10, the fasciculus cuneatus is absent at this level (it appears only at and above T6, situated lateral to fasciculus gracilis).
pearl: Fasciculus gracilis is medial and present throughout the entire spinal cord (carries lower extremities below T6). Fasciculus cuneatus is lateral and present only at and above T6 (carries upper extremities).

stem: A 60-year-old woman with chronic hypertension suffers an ischemic stroke resulting in complete loss of all somatosensory modalities (touch, vibration, proprioception, pain, and temperature) across the entire left side of her body and limbs, with relative preservation of facial sensation. An axial brain MRI reveals a lacunar infarct in the lateral nuclear mass of the right thalamus. In which specific thalamic nucleus do ascending second-order fibers of both the medial lemniscus and spinothalamic tract terminate?
rationale: The ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus is the primary somatosensory relay nucleus for the body. Both the medial lemniscus (transmitting touch, vibration, and proprioception from the contralateral body) and the spinothalamic tract (transmitting pain and temperature from the contralateral body) terminate by synapsing on third-order neurons within the VPL. In contrast, somatosensory inputs from the head and face (via trigeminal pathways) terminate in the ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus.
pearl: Somatosensory thalamic relays: VPL = Body (Ventral Postero-Lateral for Limbs); VPM = Face (Ventral Postero-Medial for Mouth/Make-up).

stem: A neuroanatomist traces the ascending medial lemniscus through serial transverse brainstem sections from the medulla to the rostral midbrain. How does the spatial orientation of the medial lemniscus shift as it ascends from the rostral medulla into the pons and midbrain?

choices.A: It remains vertically oriented along the midline across the entire brainstem
choices.B: It shifts into the ventricular floor of the fourth ventricle and enters the cerebellum
choices.C: It decussates again in the midbrain tegmentum before entering the epithalamus
choices.D: It rotates from a vertical midline position in the medulla to a horizontal transverse ribbon in the ventral pontine tegmentum, and shifts dorsolaterally in the midbrain
choices.E: It descends into the pyramids to merge with the corticospinal tract

rationale: In the rostral medulla, the medial lemniscus is oriented vertically on either side of the midline (paramedian). As it ascends into the pons, it rotates 90 degrees to form a flat, horizontal ribbon lying transversely along the boundary between the basilar pons and the pontine tegmentum. In the midbrain, it is displaced dorsolaterally, lying in the tegmentum lateral to the red nucleus and dorsolateral to the substantia nigra, before entering the VPL nucleus of the thalamus.
pearl: Medial lemniscus orientation shift: Vertical in medulla (paramedian) $ ightarrow$ Horizontal in pontine tegmentum $ ightarrow$ Dorsolateral in midbrain tegmentum.

stem: A 70-year-old man experiences an embolic stroke in the territory of the left middle cerebral artery. On physical examination, he has dense loss of two-point discrimination, graphesthesia, and stereognosis in his right hand and face. An MRI demonstrates an infarction confined to the parietal cortex immediately posterior to the central sulcus. What is the primary anatomical designation and Brodmann cytoarchitectonic classification of this cortical structure?

choices.B: Superior temporal gyrus; Brodmann areas 41 and 42

rationale: The primary somatosensory cortex (S1) is located in the postcentral gyrus of the anterior parietal lobe, bounded rostrally by the central sulcus and caudally by the postcentral sulcus. It comprises Brodmann areas 3 (3a and 3b), 1, and 2. It receives thalamocortical projections from the VPL (body) and VPM (face) via the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Lesions of the primary somatosensory cortex result in loss of discriminative touch, stereognosis, two-point discrimination, and conscious proprioception in the contralateral body.
pearl: Postcentral gyrus = Primary somatosensory cortex (S1, Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2); receives third-order thalamocortical fibers from VPL/VPM.

stem: An axial T1-weighted brain MRI shows a localized lacunar infarction in the subcortical white matter between the thalamus and the lentiform nucleus (globus pallidus and putamen). The patient exhibits contralateral hemianesthesia and contralateral hemiparesis. Through which specific anatomical subdivision of the internal capsule do third-order somatosensory fibers travel from the VPL/VPM of the thalamus to the primary somatosensory cortex?

choices.A: Posterior limb of the internal capsule
choices.B: Anterior limb of the internal capsule
choices.D: Retrolenticular part of the internal capsule
choices.E: Sublenticular part of the internal capsule

rationale: The internal capsule is a massive two-way highway of white matter fibers: (1) Anterior limb: carries frontopontine and thalamocortical fibers connecting the mediodorsal thalamus and prefrontal cortex; (2) Genu: carries corticobulbar motor fibers to cranial nerve motor nuclei; (3) Posterior limb: situated between the thalamus medially and the lentiform nucleus laterally, carries descending corticospinal motor fibers AND ascending third-order sensory thalamocortical projections from the VPL/VPM to the postcentral gyrus. An infarct in the posterior limb causes contralateral motor weakness and sensory loss.
pearl: Posterior limb of the internal capsule = Transmits descending corticospinal motor fibers AND ascending somatosensory thalamocortical fibers (VPL/VPM $ ightarrow$ S1).

stem: A 24-year-old medical student is quizzed on cutaneous dermatomes during a clinical neurology rotation. The attending physician asks: \'Which cervical dermatome provides sensory innervation to digit 1 (the thumb) as well as the lateral aspect of the forearm and arm?\' Which dermatome is correct?
rationale: The C6 dermatome covers the lateral (radial) aspect of the arm and forearm, the thenar eminence, and the entire thumb (digit 1). In contrast, C5 covers the lateral shoulder and upper arm; C7 covers the middle finger (digits 2 and 3); C8 covers the pinky (digits 4 and 5) and medial forearm; and T1 covers the medial arm and axilla.
pearl: C6 dermatome = Digit 1 (thumb) and lateral aspect of the forearm and arm (remember: form the number "6" using your thumb and index finger).

stem: In an axial section of the caudal, closed medulla, a discrete dorsal nuclear mass receives the primary ascending axons of the fasciculus gracilis. What is this nucleus called, and what is the fate of the axons that emerge from its second-order neuronal cell bodies?

choices.A: Nucleus cuneatus; axons descend into the spinal cord as the rubrospinal tract
choices.B: Hypoglossal nucleus; axons exit ventrally as cranial nerve XII
choices.C: Nucleus gracilis; axons decussate as internal arcuate fibers to form the contralateral medial lemniscus
choices.D: Spinal trigeminal nucleus; axons ascend in the solitary tract
choices.E: Inferior vestibular nucleus; axons project to the flocculonodular lobe

rationale: The nucleus gracilis is located in the dorsal medial caudal medulla. It receives uncrossed primary sensory axons ascending in the fasciculus gracilis (carrying tactile and proprioceptive information from the lower extremities and lower trunk). Axons emerging from second-order cell bodies in nucleus gracilis sweep ventromedially across the midline as internal arcuate fibers, decussating to form the contralateral medial lemniscus.
pearl: Nucleus gracilis receives fasciculus gracilis (lower body) $ ightarrow$ Axons decussate as internal arcuate fibers $ ightarrow$ Contralateral medial lemniscus.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents with Wallenberg lateral medullary syndrome following thrombosis of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). On neurological examination, he exhibits loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of his face and on the RIGHT side of his body. Which ascending tract in the lateral tegmentum of the rostral medulla was infarcted to produce the contralateral loss of body pain and temperature?
rationale: In the lateral rostral medulla, the spinothalamic tract (part of the anterolateral system) is located in the anterolateral tegmentum, perfused by the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). Because spinothalamic fibers cross in the spinal cord near their level of entry, the spinothalamic tract in the medulla carries pain and temperature information from the *contralateral* side of the body. Infarction of the lateral medulla (PICA syndrome / Wallenberg syndrome) damages the spinothalamic tract (causing contralateral body pain/temperature loss) and the spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract (causing ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss), producing a classic "crossed" sensory deficit.
pearl: Wallenberg syndrome (PICA infarct): Lateral medulla damage to *Spinothalamic tract* (contralateral body pain/temp loss) + *Spinal trigeminal tract* (ipsilateral facial pain/temp loss).

stem: A 40-year-old woman undergoes neurological testing for fine tactile discrimination. She is tested with two fine compass points applied simultaneously to the skin. The minimum distance at which two separate points can be perceived as distinct is approximately 2 to 3 mm on the fingertip, but over 40 mm on the back. Which factor primarily determines this profound difference in two-point discrimination threshold between the fingertips and the back?

choices.A: The presence of unmyelinated C fibers in the back
choices.B: Total thickness of the stratum corneum in glabrous skin
choices.C: Conduction velocity of peripheral A-alpha fibers
choices.D: The diameter of the posterior cerebral artery
choices.E: Mechanoreceptor density and the size of peripheral receptive fields, reflected by the volume of primary somatosensory cortex dedicated to that body part

rationale: Two-point discrimination threshold is the minimum physical separation between two simultaneous tactile stimuli required to perceive them as two distinct contacts. It depends on two interrelated anatomical factors: (1) Receptor density: the fingertips have a high density of Meissner corpuscles and Merkel discs with small, discrete receptive fields (1–2 mm), allowing independent activation of separate primary afferents; and (2) Cortical representation: the high peripheral receptor density is mapped to a disproportionately massive cortical area on the somatosensory homunculus in the postcentral gyrus. In contrast, the back has low receptor density and large receptive fields, resulting in poor spatial acuity.
pearl: Fine two-point discrimination depends on high mechanoreceptor density, small receptive fields, and a large dedicated cortical representation in S1.

stem: A cross-section through the caudal pons at the level of the facial colliculus is examined. A ribbon of ascending white matter fibers lies horizontally in the ventral tegmentum, immediately dorsal to the basilar pons. The fibers originating from the contralateral lower extremity (derived from nucleus gracilis) occupy which position within this horizontal medial lemniscus ribbon?

choices.C: Dorsal-most position along the ventricular floor
choices.E: Deep inside the superior olivary complex

rationale: Somatotopic organization within the medial lemniscus rotates as it ascends: In the medulla, leg fibers (from nucleus gracilis) are ventral and arm fibers (from nucleus cuneatus) are dorsal. In the pons, as the lemniscus rotates to a horizontal ribbon, the fibers flip: lower extremity fibers (sacral/lumbar) shift to the *lateral* part of the medial lemniscus, while upper extremity fibers (cervical) occupy the *medial* part. In the midbrain, this lateral position of the leg fibers is maintained as it approaches the VPL thalamus.
pearl: Medial lemniscus somatotopy in the pons: Leg fibers are *lateral*; Arm fibers are *medial*.

stem: A neuroanatomical specimen of the human spinal cord is prepared with a Nissl stain. A prominent nuclear column of large neurons is observed in the medial base of the dorsal horn (Rexed lamina VII), extending from C8 down to L3. What is this nucleus, and which sensory pathway originates from its cell bodies?

choices.A: Substantia gelatinosa; origin of the anterior spinothalamic tract
choices.B: Clarke\'s nucleus (nucleus dorsalis); origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract
choices.C: Intermediolateral cell column; origin of preganglionic parasympathetic fibers
choices.D: Nucleus cuneatus; origin of the medial lemniscus
choices.E: Nucleus ambiguus; origin of special visceral efferent fibers

rationale: Clarke\'s column (nucleus dorsalis of Clarke) is a prominent column of large round neurons located in the medial base of the dorsal horn in Rexed lamina VII. It is present exclusively from spinal segments C8 down to L3. It receives unconscious proprioceptive inputs from muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs of the ipsilateral lower extremity and trunk. Its second-order axons ascend uncrossed in the lateral funiculus as the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (DSCT), entering the cerebellum via the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
pearl: Clarke\'s column (C8–L3, lamina VII): Relays unconscious proprioception from the lower body to the cerebellum via the *dorsal spinocerebellar tract*.

stem: A 50-year-old man undergoes sensory testing. A wisp of cotton is brushed lightly across his anterior chest wall at the horizontal level of the nipples, and across his abdomen at the level of the umbilicus. Which spinal cord segments are evaluated by testing these two landmark dermatomes?
rationale: Landmark thoracic dermatomes are standard board testing points: T4 is located at the horizontal line connecting the nipples ("T4 at the teat"), and T10 is located at the horizontal level of the umbilicus ("T10 at the belly but-ten").
pearl: Nipple dermatome = T4; Umbilicus dermatome = T10; Inguinal crease = L1.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with severe tingling and numbness along the medial side of her hand, ring finger, and little finger. Physical examination confirms sensory loss strictly confined to digits 4 and 5, extending along the medial forearm. Triceps reflex is normal, but she has mild weakness of finger abduction. Which cervical nerve root dermatome corresponds to the medial hand and little finger?
rationale: The C8 dermatome provides sensory innervation to the medial (ulnar) side of the hand, including the little finger (digit 5) and medial half of the ring finger (digit 4), extending onto the distal medial forearm. In contrast, C6 innervates the thumb and radial forearm; C7 innervates the middle finger; and T1 innervates the proximal medial forearm and arm.
pearl: Hand dermatomes: C6 = Thumb (digit 1); C7 = Middle finger (digits 2–3); C8 = Pinky / little finger (digits 4–5).

stem: A 35-year-old man is brought to the clinic following a diving accident resulting in a cervical spine fracture. Neurological examination reveals that pinprick and thermal sensations are completely preserved on his right side, but he cannot feel pinprick or hot/cold stimuli on his entire left body below the C6 dermatome. Where in the spinal cord is the lesion located, and on which side?

choices.D: Bilateral anterior white commissure at C5–C6

rationale: The spinothalamic tract / anterolateral system (ALS) carries pain and temperature information that has already crossed the midline in the anterior white commissure approximately 1 to 2 segments above entry. Therefore, sensory loss of pain and temperature on the LEFT side of the body below C6 signifies a lesion in the *contralateral* (RIGHT) anterolateral system at or slightly above the C6 level (i.e., at C4–C5).
pearl: Loss of pain and temperature on one side of the body indicates a lesion in the *contralateral* anterolateral system (ALS) 1–2 segments above the sensory level.

stem: A patient with an infarct in the primary somatosensory cortex has difficulty identifying common objects (such as a key or a coin) placed in his right hand when his eyes are closed, despite having normal primary touch detection. What is the clinical term for this high-level cortical tactile deficit, and in which cortical region is this synthesis performed?

choices.A: Astereognosis (tactile agnosia); Somatosensory association cortex (Brodmann areas 5 and 7 in superior parietal lobule)
choices.C: Tabetic ataxia; Vermis of the cerebellum
choices.D: Prosopagnosia; Fusiform face area in temporal lobe

rationale: Astereognosis (tactile agnosia) is the inability to identify an object by active touch and manipulation in the absence of visual input, despite relatively intact primary touch sensation. Primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, areas 3, 1, 2) extracts basic tactile features (shape, edges, texture) and projects them to the adjacent somatosensory association cortex in the superior parietal lobule (Brodmann areas 5 and 7). Here, these elementary features are integrated into a three-dimensional mental concept of the object. Damage to areas 5 and 7 or the primary sensory cortex produces astereognosis.
pearl: Astereognosis = Inability to identify an object by touch with eyes closed; indicates dysfunction of the contralateral parietal somatosensory cortex (areas 5 and 7).

stem: A researcher performs electrical recordings along the dorsal surface of the human brainstem. At the level of the open medulla, the fourth ventricle floor (rhomboid fossa) is exposed. Which landmark sulcus on the ventricular floor marks the boundary between the medial somatic motor nuclei (e.g., hypoglossal trigone) and the lateral sensory nuclei (e.g., vestibular area)?
rationale: The sulcus limitans is an essential developmental and anatomical groove that extends along the floor of the fourth ventricle. In embryonic development, the sulcus limitans separates the dorsal alar plate (sensory) from the ventral basal plate (motor). In the adult brainstem, structures derived from the basal plate (somatic and visceral motor nuclei, such as the hypoglossal nucleus and motor nucleus of the vagus) lie *medial* to the sulcus limitans, whereas structures derived from the alar plate (sensory nuclei, such as the vestibular nuclei and solitary nucleus) lie *lateral* to the sulcus limitans.
pearl: Sulcus limitans on the floor of the 4th ventricle separates medial motor nuclei (basal plate) from lateral sensory nuclei (alar plate).

stem: A 55-year-old man undergoes cross-sectional imaging of the spinal cord. In the thoracic spinal cord, the gray matter contains the intermediolateral cell column in the lateral horn. Which type of neuronal cell bodies are located in the lateral horn from T1 to L2?

choices.A: Somatic alpha motor neurons supplying limb muscles
choices.E: Gamma motor neurons supplying intrafusal muscle spindles

rationale: The lateral horn (intermediolateral cell column, IML) is present in the spinal cord from segments T1 to L2/L3. It contains the cell bodies of preganglionic sympathetic autonomic neurons. Their myelinated axons exit the spinal cord via the ventral roots and travel in white rami communicantes to reach the paravertebral sympathetic chain ganglia. (A similar parasympathetic autonomic nucleus is located in the sacral cord at S2–S4, but does not form a distinct lateral horn).
pearl: Lateral horn of the spinal cord (T1–L2) = Intermediolateral cell column containing *preganglionic sympathetic neurons*.

stem: A 30-year-old woman is tested with a pinprick along her lower extremity. The sharp sensation is mediated by primary afferents that enter the spinal cord and decussate to ascend in the spinothalamic tract. Through which anatomical structure do these second-order nociceptive axons decussate in the spinal cord?
rationale: Primary nociceptive axons (A-delta and C fibers) enter via dorsal roots, ascend/descend 1–2 segments in Lissauer\'s tract, and synapse on second-order neurons in the dorsal horn (laminae I, II, and V). Axons of these second-order projection neurons then cross the midline obliquely within the anterior (ventral) white commissure, located immediately ventral to the central canal, before entering the contralateral anterolateral funiculus to ascend as the spinothalamic tract.
pearl: Spinothalamic second-order fibers decussate in the *anterior white commissure* of the spinal cord (unlike DCML, which decussates as internal arcuate fibers in the medulla).

stem: A 65-year-old woman is examined for balance instability. When she stands with her eyes open, she is steady. When she closes her eyes, she sways and loses her balance (positive Romberg test). However, when her finger-to-nose and rapid alternating movements are tested with her eyes open, they are smooth, rapid, and accurate. Which statement accurately contrasts sensory ataxia from cerebellar ataxia?

choices.A: Cerebellar ataxia causes instability only with eyes closed, whereas sensory ataxia causes instability with eyes open and closed
choices.B: Sensory ataxia is accompanied by intention tremor, whereas cerebellar ataxia has no tremor
choices.C: Sensory ataxia causes unsteadiness when eyes are open, which disappears when eyes are closed
choices.D: Sensory ataxia is caused by a lesion in the spinothalamic tract, whereas cerebellar ataxia is caused by an anterior horn lesion
choices.E: Sensory ataxia causes instability specifically when visual compensation is removed (eyes closed), whereas cerebellar ataxia causes instability and dysmetria with eyes both open and closed

rationale: In sensory (proprioceptive) ataxia (caused by dorsal column or large-fiber peripheral nerve lesions), the patient relies heavily on visual feedback to compensate for absent joint position sense. When eyes are open, the patient can maintain balance; when eyes are closed, visual compensation is removed and the patient sways or falls (positive Romberg sign). In cerebellar ataxia (caused by lesions of the cerebellar vermis or hemispheres), motor coordination and equilibrium circuits are intrinsically damaged; consequently, the patient is ataxic, unsteady, and exhibits dysmetria with eyes BOTH open and closed (negative Romberg, because closing the eyes does not significantly worsen the unsteadiness).
pearl: Romberg test: Positive in *sensory ataxia* (dorsal columns: unsteady with eyes closed, steady with eyes open); Negative in *cerebellar ataxia* (unsteady with eyes open AND closed).
